changes.value: First pass: every process of the decomposition, guessed at every date.

Second pass, level 3 of the time schedule: every process guessed at -180000 (the penultimate glacial), -60000 (the end of MIS 4, around the dispersal out of Africa), -37000 (MIS 3), -12000 (about 14,000 years ago, the Bølling–Allerød warm interval), -6300 (about 8,300 years ago, early farming and the 8.2 ka cold event) and 1400 (after the Black Death). Each is guessed within its neighbours. Two corrections: religion shares before 1000 BCE were linear interpolations between anchors at -300000 and -1000 that put Hindu and Chinese-tradition shares into the Palaeolithic, now local and folk traditions 100%; and global temperature at -10000 (the Younger Dryas) lowered from -1.5 to -2.8 °C. Bands are judged per value rather than by the first pass's formula, whose floor made tiny quantities' bands meaningless.

changes.value: Level 4 of the time schedule, batch A: the root, humanity, the Earth's processes and the demographic processes, at the 33 dates of the finest level. The root (billions ever born) is re-derived at every date: its first-pass series followed the Population Reference Bureau's total of about 117 billion, whose pre-modern birth rate of 80 per 1,000 implies a life expectancy near 12, against this model's own 25 to 30, and whose 1950–2000 increment here (14.5 billion) was more than twice what population times birth rate gives (about 6). It is now the integral of h.humanity times a crude birth rate consistent with h.alive (34 per 1,000 for foragers, 38 to 40 for farmers, falling from 37 in 1950 to 16.5 in 2025), counted from about 320,000 years ago, with the Bureau's account inside the upper band. Women's age at marriage in 1400 raised from 17.2 to 17.7 so it no longer dips below 1300.

upsert.boundary: History: the lifecycle of the Universe
upsert.description: History, the lifecycle of the Universe, followed here from 300,000 years ago to the end of 2025 for the Earth and humanity. Its processes, every one a node of one decomposition rooted at the process history, are guessed at 73 dates each: densest in the last two centuries, sparsest in the Pleistocene. It contains every other Event the account will record.

value.description: A cold interval inside the deglaciation.

inferred: farming began independently in at least six regions within a few millennia after the Holocene began, and nowhere in the hundred thousand years before; a stable, warmer, CO2-richer climate made cultivation reliable.
provenance: inferred: the independent origins all fall in the Holocene

upsert.boundary: The Antonine plague, 165 to 180.
upsert.description: Probably smallpox, brought back by Roman armies from the east; it kills perhaps a tenth of the Roman empire's people over fifteen years.
provenance: inferred: the toll is contested, from 2% to over 20%

upsert.boundary: The Black Death, 1346 to 1353.
upsert.description: Plague crosses from the steppe to the Black Sea at Caffa in 1346 and sweeps the Mediterranean, Europe and the Middle East, killing perhaps a third to a half of their people. Survivors have more land and higher wages; towns are hit hardest.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the toll outside Europe and the Middle East is poorly known

upsert.boundary: The Columbian exchange and the collapse of the Americas, 1492 to 1650.
upsert.description: Contact joins the hemispheres. Smallpox, measles and other diseases kill most of the Americas' people, perhaps 50 million falling to under 10; their fields return to forest. American maize, potatoes and cassava later feed growth across Afro-Eurasia.
provenance: inferred: the Americas' 1492 population is contested, from about 8 to over 100 million

upsert.boundary: Concorde's scheduled service, January 1976 to October 2003.
upsert.description: Supersonic passenger flights at about 2,150 km/h between Europe and North America; after the 2000 crash and the 2001 slump it is retired, and the fastest regular passenger speed falls back to the subsonic jet's.

upsert.boundary: The COVID-19 pandemic, 2020 to May 2023.
upsert.description: About 15 to 20 million excess deaths; world life expectancy falls by nearly two years by 2021 and recovers by 2023.

upsert.boundary: The last deglaciation, about 19,000 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: The world warms about 6 °C, sea level rises about 70 m through meltwater pulses, CO2 rises to about 260 ppm. People enter the Americas, and in south-west Asia sedentary foragers begin cultivating wild cereals.

upsert.boundary: The main dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa, about 60,000 to 45,000 years ago.
upsert.description: Small groups leave Africa, meet and interbreed with Neanderthals about 47,000 years ago, and reach South Asia, Sahul and Europe. Earlier ventures, such as those at Misliya and Skhul, left few or no living descendants. When Sahul was reached is contested: 65,000 years at Madjedebe, or about 50,000, which would fit the shared Neanderthal admixture.
provenance: inferred: genomic and archaeological chronology as recalled; the start date is contested

upsert.boundary: The first states, cities and writing, about 3500 to 2500 BCE.
upsert.description: In Mesopotamia and Egypt, then the Indus, rulers tax, keep records in writing and command armies; Uruk passes 40,000 people. Hereditary rank becomes the rule wherever states form.

upsert.boundary: The influenza pandemic, 1918 to 1920.
upsert.description: Three waves kill perhaps 25 to 50 million, more than the war, most in India.

upsert.boundary: The Great Chinese Famine, 1959 to 1961.
upsert.description: Caused by the Great Leap Forward's procurement and collectivization, not by weather alone: 15 to 45 million excess deaths. World life expectancy dips.

upsert.boundary: The fall of the Han and the Three Kingdoms, 184 to 280.
upsert.description: The Yellow Turban rising, warlord wars and the Three Kingdoms: China's registered population falls from about 56 million to about 16 million, partly a collapse of registration, partly real loss. Jin reunifies China in 280.
provenance: inferred: census figures as recalled; the real loss is uncertain

upsert.boundary: The industrial revolution in Britain, about 1760 to 1840.
upsert.description: Coal-fired steam, mechanized textiles and iron, then railways: the first economy to draw its energy from a stock rather than from land. Output per person begins to grow faster than population for generations.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; why it began in Britain is contested

upsert.boundary: The first wave of the Justinianic plague, 541 to 549.
upsert.description: Yersinia pestis, confirmed in sixth-century graves, reaches the Mediterranean from Egypt in 541; it returns in waves until about 750. Its toll is contested, from a few percent to a third or more of the empire's people.

upsert.boundary: The Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago.
upsert.description: Ice sheets at their greatest extent, sea level about 125 m below today, CO2 about 188 ppm. People abandon northern Europe and Siberia for refugia; the Bering land bridge is open.

upsert.boundary: The Ming–Qing transition, 1618 to 1683.
upsert.description: From the Jurchen declaration of war on the Ming to the Qing conquest of Taiwan: rebellion, invasion and famine, in the coldest decades of the Little Ice Age, cost China perhaps 25 million lives. It overlaps the Thirty Years War in Europe.

upsert.boundary: The Mongol conquests, 1206 to 1279.
upsert.description: From Chinggis Khan's election in 1206 to the fall of the Southern Song in 1279, the largest contiguous land empire is built through wars that kill millions in northern China, Central Asia and Iran. The empire joins the steppe routes from China to the Black Sea.

upsert.boundary: The origins and spread of farming, from about 9700 to 3000 BCE.
upsert.description: Plants and animals are domesticated independently in south-west Asia, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes and Africa, and farming spreads out from them, mostly by the movement of farming peoples. Farmers live at far higher densities than foragers, work longer and are shorter and sicker; once their numbers depend on it the practice cannot be given up.

upsert.boundary: The Taiping war, 1850 to 1864.
upsert.description: A millenarian rebellion and the Qing response devastate the Yangtze valley; with the famine and disease that followed it killed perhaps 20 to 30 million, the deadliest war of the nineteenth century.

upsert.boundary: Termination II: the end of the penultimate glacial, about 136,000 to 129,000 years ago.
upsert.description: Ice sheets collapse, sea level rises about 100 m, CO2 climbs from about 190 to 275 ppm and the world warms into the Last Interglacial, briefly warmer than pre-industrial. A green Sahara and Arabia open corridors out of Africa.
provenance: inferred: palaeoclimate chronology as recalled (marine isotope stage 6 to 5e)

upsert.boundary: The First World War, 1914 to November 1918.
upsert.description: About 9 to 10 million soldiers and some 7 million civilians die.

upsert.boundary: The Second World War, September 1939 to September 1945.
upsert.description: With the Sino-Japanese war already under way, it kills about 70 to 85 million, most of them civilians, the largest share in the Soviet Union and China. Governments take over a third or more of national output.

upsert.boundary: The Younger Dryas, about 12,900 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: A return to near-glacial cold in the north Atlantic region, with drought in the Levant; globally a pause in warming rather than a reversal. Its end is the start of the Holocene.

The other answers to the same question are security, family and faith, and freedom and self-expression. changes.value: The number test found that the process labelled "What matters to people" (h.ends) holds a development index of life, literacy and income, which claims more than it measures. That node heads nine dimensions (staying alive, sustenance, belonging, understanding, play, standing, freedom, meaning, continuation), so it needs a measure of what matters to people. This opens h.wants: the share of people whose first want for their lives is survival. That is one answer of the number test's question of what people most want (survival / security / family and faith / freedom and self-expression), carried as a value with a unit. The index is then filed under it under its own name, in the next revision.

China's escape from poverty moves the world total most.
COVID-19 and its slump push some back toward survival-first; read as a pause rather than a turn.
About one person in five still puts survival first: more than the 8.5% in extreme poverty, since many above that line still live close to it.

The nine dimensions it headed, with the index itself, now sit under h.wants, 'What matters to people', which carries a measure of what people want for their lives. upsert.boundary: The movement to abolish the slave trade and slavery, 1787 to 1888.
upsert.description: From the London committee of 1787 and the Haitian revolution of 1791 to Brazil's Golden Law of 1888: Britain abolishes the trade in 1807 and slavery in its colonies in 1834, and its navy suppresses the Atlantic trade.

upsert.boundary: Aerosol pollution, from about 1850 to now.
upsert.description: Sulphate and other particles from burning coal and oil reflect sunlight and brighten clouds, masking part of the warming; cleaner air since the 1980s in Europe and North America, and since about 2010 in China and in shipping, removes part of the mask.
provenance: inferred: IPCC AR6 attribution, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The Americas cut off from Afro-Eurasia, from about 16,000 years ago to 1492.
upsert.description: People enter the Americas across Beringia before rising seas close it. With few domesticated animals (dogs, llamas, guinea pigs, turkeys) the Americas never breed the crowd diseases that Afro-Eurasia's herds gave its people, and no traveller brings them across: smallpox, measles and influenza find no immunity in 1492.

upsert.boundary: Antibiotics, from sulfa drugs (1935) to now.
upsert.description: Sulfonamides, then penicillin from 1942 and streptomycin from 1944, cure pneumonia, sepsis, puerperal fever and tuberculosis, which had been the commonest killers of adults.

upsert.boundary: The end of the African Humid Period, about 4000 to 3000 BCE.
upsert.description: The Sahara and Arabia dry out again over a millennium; herders and farmers move toward the Nile, the Tigris and the Euphrates, crowding the valleys where the first states form.
provenance: exploring: the link between drying and state formation is argued, notably for Egypt, and contested

upsert.boundary: The Atlantic economy enriches north-west Europe, about 1600 to 1760.
upsert.description: Colonies, sugar, tobacco and the slave trade, with the trade of the Indies, make London and Amsterdam the richest cities of their time; in Britain wages are high and coal is cheap, so machines that save labour by using energy pay there first.
provenance: exploring: the high-wage, cheap-energy account (Allen's) is one of several rival accounts of why industry began in Britain

upsert.boundary: Britain turns to coal, about 1560 to 1760.
upsert.description: As wood grows dear, London and the British towns heat, brew, bake and smelt with coal from seams near water: output rises from perhaps a quarter of a million to about five million tonnes a year, more than the rest of Europe together. Mines need pumping, which is where the steam engine is first used.

upsert.boundary: China's reform and opening, from 1978 to now.
upsert.description: Household farming replaces the communes, prices are freed, and coastal zones open to foreign trade and capital; China's output per person grows about twentyfold, and some 800 million people leave extreme poverty.

upsert.boundary: Carbon dioxide rises from 278 ppm (1750) to 427 ppm (2025).
upsert.description: About 2,500 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide are emitted, from fossil fuels and cement and from clearing land; a little under half stays in the air, and the ocean and land take up the rest.
provenance: inferred: the Global Carbon Project's budget, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The end of the Cold War, 1989 to 1991.
upsert.description: The Soviet bloc's regimes fall in 1989 and the Soviet Union dissolves in December 1991; most of central and eastern Europe holds free elections.

upsert.boundary: Modern contraception and family planning, from 1960 to now.
upsert.description: The pill (1960), the IUD and sterilization, with national family-planning programmes from India (1952) to Bangladesh and Iran: by 2025 most women of reproductive age who are married use a modern method.

upsert.boundary: COVID-19 vaccines, December 2020 to May 2023.
upsert.description: Vaccines developed within a year are given as over 13 billion doses by 2023.

upsert.boundary: The Crimean War, 1853 to 1856.
upsert.description: Russia is defeated by Britain, France and the Ottoman empire; its rulers conclude that a state of serfs cannot field a modern army or economy.

upsert.boundary: Decolonization, 1945 to 1975.
upsert.description: From Indonesia and India to Angola and Mozambique, about eighty colonies become independent states; some keep elected government, many do not.

upsert.boundary: Democracy with broad suffrage spreads, 1945 to 2025.
upsert.description: From about 8% of people in 1945 to 30% by 1960, when India's elections count, about 55% around 2000, and 48% by 2025 after backsliding.

upsert.boundary: Clearing for farms before 1700, from about 7900 BCE.
upsert.description: Farmers clear forest for fields and pasture as farming spreads and populations grow, in Europe, China, India and the Middle East above all; much of it by 1700, before industry.
provenance: exploring: how much forest pre-industrial farming cleared is disputed; KK10-type reconstructions give far more than HYDE

upsert.boundary: Slavery and serfdom abolished in law across most of the world, 1800 to 1900.
upsert.description: The share of people held as slaves, serfs or forced labourers falls from about 7% to 2%: the British, French and Dutch empires, India (1843), Russia (1861), the United States (1865), Brazil (1888) and others end bondage in law, though forced labour persists in colonies and beyond the law.

upsert.boundary: The escape from extreme poverty, 1950 to 2025.
upsert.description: The share of people in extreme poverty falls from about 55% to 8.5%, the number from about 1.4 billion to about 0.7 billion while population more than triples: most of the fall after 1980, and most of that in China, then India and the rest of Asia.
provenance: inferred: the model's own poverty share; numbers as recalled

upsert.boundary: Adults stop dying of infection, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Tuberculosis, typhoid, cholera, smallpox, malaria and pneumonia, the commonest killers of young and middle-aged adults in 1900, become rare causes of death outside the poorest countries.

upsert.boundary: Children stop dying of infection, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Deaths before age five, mostly from diarrhoea, pneumonia, measles, malaria and neonatal infection, fall from about 38% of children born to 3.6%.

upsert.boundary: Deaths from heart disease and stroke are postponed, 1965 to 2025.
upsert.description: Less smoking, blood-pressure and cholesterol drugs, and emergency and surgical care cut age-specific deaths from cardiovascular disease by half or more in rich countries, and less elsewhere.

upsert.boundary: Famine nearly ends, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Famines killed tens of millions until the 1960s; since then their tolls are a small fraction, and undernourishment, which raises deaths from infection, falls from about half of people to under a tenth.

upsert.boundary: Mothers stop dying in childbirth, 1900 to 2025.
upsert.description: Maternal deaths fall from perhaps 1 in 100 births to about 1 in 4,000, and with fewer births each woman faces the risk fewer times.

upsert.boundary: The fertility transition, 1965 to 2025.
upsert.description: World fertility falls from about 5 children per woman to 2.2, first in East Asia and Latin America, then South Asia, then, more slowly, Africa.

upsert.boundary: The world loses about a third of its forest, 7900 BCE to 2025.
upsert.description: Forest falls from about 45% of land to 31%: slowly as farming spreads, then quickly in the temperate frontiers after 1700 and in the tropics after 1950.
provenance: inferred: the model's own forest series

upsert.boundary: Burning fossil fuels, from about 1760 to now.
upsert.description: Coal, then oil and gas, from Britain's engines to about 37 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide a year in 2025; with cement, about 1,800 billion tonnes since 1750.
provenance: inferred: the Global Carbon Project's totals, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The germ theory of disease, 1857 to 1890.
upsert.description: Pasteur, Lister and Koch show that microbes cause infection and identify the bacteria of anthrax, tuberculosis and cholera; boiling, antisepsis and hygiene follow from it, and later vaccines and antibiotics.

upsert.boundary: The Glorious Revolution, 1688 to 1689.
upsert.description: Parliament becomes supreme in England; property and public debt are secured by law, and the Bank of England follows in 1694.
provenance: exploring: how much the settlement mattered to growth is disputed (North and Weingast against later critics)

upsert.boundary: The Great Famine of northern Europe, 1315 to 1322.
upsert.description: Years of rain ruin harvests, and a cattle plague follows: perhaps a tenth of northern Europe's people die, and the children of these years grow up undernourished, a generation before the plague.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the claim that famine-born cohorts died more readily of plague is argued from skeletons and is exploring

upsert.boundary: The Great Leap Forward, 1958 to 1960.
upsert.description: Mao's campaign collectivizes farming into communes, diverts labour to steel, and procures grain on inflated harvest reports; after the Lushan conference of 1959 the reports cannot be questioned.

upsert.boundary: The green revolution, 1960 to 2000.
upsert.description: High-yielding wheat and rice, with fertilizer and irrigation, double and triple cereal yields across Asia and Latin America; food per person rises while population doubles.

upsert.boundary: Synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, from 1913 to now.
upsert.description: The Haber–Bosch process fixes nitrogen from the air: from the first plant at Oppau in 1913 to over 100 million tonnes of fixed nitrogen a year, on which perhaps two fifths to a half of the food people eat depends.

upsert.boundary: The Holocene, from 11,700 years ago to now.
upsert.description: An interglacial whose climate stays within about a degree of its mean for ten thousand years, with carbon dioxide between 260 and 280 ppm, unlike the swings of the glacial before it. Every independent origin of farming falls inside it.
provenance: inferred: ice-core and stacked temperature reconstructions, as recalled

upsert.boundary: A wetter window in north-east Africa and Arabia, about 60,000 to 55,000 years ago.
upsert.description: After the cold, dry Marine Isotope Stage 4, rainfall returns for a time to parts of the Horn of Africa and the Arabian corridor, so groups can cross what is otherwise desert.
provenance: exploring: humid phases in Arabia are dated mostly to earlier interglacials; one this late is supported by fewer records

upsert.boundary: India's democracy, from its constitution of 1950 to now.
upsert.description: Universal adult suffrage from the first election of 1951–52: the largest electorate on Earth, suspended only in the Emergency of 1975–77. India alone is about a sixth of humanity.

upsert.boundary: India's liberalization, from 1991 to now.
upsert.description: After a balance-of-payments crisis India ends industrial licensing and opens to trade; growth roughly doubles to 6 or 7% a year.

upsert.boundary: Irrigation farming on the Mesopotamian alluvium, about 6000 to 3500 BCE.
upsert.description: In the Ubaid and Uruk periods farmers canal the Euphrates onto the plain, so yields far exceed rain-fed fields but depend on works and land that cannot be left: people are tied to the valley, the condition ExitCage#eef7 describes.

upsert.boundary: World life expectancy rises from 32 years (1900) to 73.5 (2025).
upsert.description: The mortality transition: deaths of children from infection fall first and most, then those of adults from tuberculosis and other infections, famine almost ends, and after 1970 deaths from heart disease and stroke are postponed. 41.5 years are gained.
provenance: inferred: the model's own life expectancy and child mortality

upsert.boundary: Literacy rises from 6% of adults (1500) to 87.5% (2025).
upsert.description: Slowly in north-west Europe after printing and the Reformation, then everywhere with mass schooling after 1870 and above all after 1950.
provenance: inferred: the model's own literacy series

upsert.boundary: The Little Ice Age, about 1300 to 1850.
upsert.description: Cooler centuries, coldest in the 1600s, with failed harvests from China to Europe in its worst decades; a few tenths of a degree globally, more in the northern lands.

upsert.boundary: No war between great powers, from September 1945 to 2025.
upsert.description: Eighty years without war between great powers, the longest such stretch since the states system began; war deaths fall from about 500 per 100,000 a year in the world war to 1 to 2 in most later decades, though Korea, Vietnam, the Iran–Iraq war, Congo and Ukraine kill millions.
provenance: inferred: the model's own war series

upsert.boundary: Mass schooling, from about 1870 to now.
upsert.description: Compulsory, state-funded primary schooling spreads from Prussia, Britain (1870), France and the United States, then to the colonies and, after 1950, to almost every country; girls' schooling catches up with boys' in most of the world by 2000.

upsert.boundary: Medieval growth, about 1000 to 1300.
upsert.description: Europe's people roughly double, China grows under the Song, and Islamic lands are densely settled: by 1300 much of Eurasia is at the limit its land and techniques can feed (MalthusianTrap#0f6b), with towns linked by long-distance trade.

upsert.boundary: Still Bay and Howiesons Poort, about 77,000 to 59,000 years ago.
upsert.description: In southern Africa people make hafted microliths, heat-treat stone, engrave ochre and wear shell beads, then the toolkits fade and return: an instance of CumulativeCulture#4f93, held where populations were large and connected and lost where they were not. It shows the skills that later let small groups live in new lands.
provenance: exploring: whether these industries mark a change that made the dispersal possible is argued, not settled

upsert.boundary: The Natufian, about 15,000 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: In the Levant foragers settle in stone houses, bury their dead in villages and harvest wild cereals with sickles: the first dense, sedentary populations, which the cold, dry Younger Dryas then strains.

upsert.boundary: Nuclear weapons, from 1945 to now.
upsert.description: From Hiroshima, then the Soviet bomb of 1949, to some 12,000 warheads in nine states: a war between great powers could now destroy both.

upsert.boundary: World population grows from 1.65 billion (1900) to 8.19 billion (2025).
upsert.description: Deaths fall a generation or more before births (DemographicTransition#6e31), so 6.5 billion people are added in 125 years, most of them in Asia and Africa after 1950.

upsert.boundary: The postwar order, from 1944 to now.
upsert.description: Bretton Woods (1944), the United Nations (1945), the GATT (1947) and the American alliances: open trade among most market economies, and institutions in which great powers settle disputes short of war.

upsert.boundary: Printing with movable type spreads across Europe, 1450 to 1500.
upsert.description: From Mainz, presses reach some 250 European towns by 1500 and print perhaps twenty million volumes: books fall in price by an order of magnitude.

upsert.boundary: The Reformation, 1517 to 1648.
upsert.description: Protestant churches ask every believer to read scripture; Protestant lands, and Catholic ones competing with them, open schools.

upsert.boundary: Russia emancipates its serfs, March 1861.
upsert.description: About 23 million privately held serfs become free in law, with land they must buy back over 49 years; the state peasants follow in 1866.

upsert.boundary: Clean water and sewers, from about 1850 to now.
upsert.description: After the cholera epidemics, London, then the cities of Europe and North America, filter and pipe water and carry sewage away (the London sewers 1859 to 1875, chlorination from 1908); after 1950 piped water spreads through the world's towns. By 2025 about three quarters of people have safely managed drinking water.

upsert.boundary: The scientific revolution, from Copernicus (1543) to Newton's Principia (1687).
upsert.description: Measurement, experiment and mathematics settle disputed claims among a network of learned societies and printed journals; by 1700 the instrument makers and engineers of north-west Europe draw on it.

upsert.boundary: The transatlantic slave trade, 1501 to 1867.
upsert.description: About 12.5 million Africans are embarked for the Americas, of whom about 10.7 million survive the crossing; the plantations they are forced to work grow the sugar and the cotton of the Atlantic economy.
provenance: inferred: the voyages database's totals, as recalled

upsert.boundary: Smallpox reaches the Caribbean in 1518 and central Mexico in 1520.
upsert.description: The first great American smallpox epidemic kills perhaps a third of the people of central Mexico within a year, during Cortés's siege of Tenochtitlan; others follow it down to the Andes before the Spanish arrive there.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; tolls are contested

upsert.boundary: The Spanish conquest of the Aztec and Inca states and the forced labour after it, 1519 to 1572.
upsert.description: From Cortés's landing in 1519 to the fall of Vilcabamba in 1572: war, enslavement, the encomienda's tribute and labour, and the silver mines' draft remove the care, food and refuge that recovery from epidemics needed.

upsert.boundary: The steam engine, from Newcomen's (1712) to Watt's rotary engine (1784).
upsert.description: Newcomen's atmospheric engine pumps coal mines; Watt's separate condenser cuts its coal use by three quarters, and the rotary engine drives mills. Energy from a stock of fossil carbon can now do work anywhere.

upsert.boundary: Clearing the temperate frontiers for farms, 1700 to 1950.
upsert.description: Forest and grassland are ploughed and grazed across North America, Russia and Siberia, Australia, Argentina, and the farmlands of India and China: farmland roughly triples.
provenance: inferred: HYDE-type land-use reconstructions, as recalled

upsert.boundary: Clearing tropical forest, 1950 to now.
upsert.description: Cattle, soy, oil palm, smallholders and logging clear forest in Amazonia, south-east Asia and central Africa.

upsert.boundary: The American Civil War and emancipation, April 1861 to December 1865.
upsert.description: The war, the Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 and the Thirteenth Amendment of December 1865 free about four million enslaved people.

upsert.boundary: Mass vaccination, from about 1920 to now.
upsert.description: Diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccines, then polio and measles; smallpox is eradicated in 1980, and the Expanded Programme on Immunization (1974) takes the basic vaccines to most of the world's children.

upsert.boundary: The world warms by about 1.45 °C, 1850 to 2025.
upsert.description: Global mean temperature, against 1850–1900, rises little until about 1910, by about 0.3 °C to the 1940s, pauses while aerosols rise, and then by about 0.2 °C a decade from 1975.

upsert.boundary: Wild cereal stands spread across the Levant and the Zagros, about 14,700 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: As the world warms and carbon dioxide rises, the wild ancestors of einkorn, emmer and barley, with lentils, peas and flax, grow densely within reach of people who also live among wild sheep, goats, cattle and pigs: more domesticable species together than anywhere else.
provenance: inferred: the founder crops' wild ranges and their deglacial expansion, as recalled

upsert.boundary: The First World War, 1914 to November 1918.
upsert.description: About 9 to 10 million soldiers and some 7 million civilians die.

value: inferred: claude, causes pass, 2026-10-11; dates and magnitudes as recalled, none checked against a source in this pass

changes.value: The causes pass. The account says what happened and how much, but hardly why. These Events are the causes, and the outcomes over many decades, that the cause readings need and the model lacked: the conditions behind the dispersal, farming and the first states; the medieval and early-modern conditions behind the Black Death, the collapse of the Americas and the industrial revolution; the sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics, fertilizer and schooling behind the mortality, population and fertility transitions; the reforms behind the escape from poverty; the political turns behind democracy and the long peace; the emancipations; the fossil fuels, clearing and aerosols behind the rise of carbon dioxide and warming. Each is placed in History, and names in process_ids the processes it moves where those carry values at its dates. The war Events now also name Safety, which is homicide plus war, so its jumps at the wars are explained.

changes.value: Five new Events begin between 1500 and 1550: the slave trade (1501), the Reformation (1517), smallpox in the Americas (1518), the Spanish conquest (1519) and the collapse they compound. Every process gets a value at 1520, guessed between its 1500 and 1550 values in light of those Events, so no curve passes over them. Where an Event moves a process, the note says how; elsewhere the value continues its line.

Two repairs. (1) Safety is homicide plus war, so the war Events move it as much as War itself: the Second World War, the Taiping war, the Ming–Qing transition and the fall of the Han now name Safety too, which explains its jumps at their dates. (2) The wetter window about 60,000 years ago is withdrawn: it was added in this pass as a possible trigger of the dispersal, but the humid phases of Arabia and north-east Africa are dated mostly to earlier interglacials, and one this late rests on too few records to name as an Event. The dispersal's trigger stays an open question (claude.question.dispersal-trigger in the graph).

The cause Events crowd ten stretches of the schedule with three or more Events: the peopling of the Americas, the Natufian and the spread of wild cereals (-13000); the Holocene's start and farming's (-9700); printing and Columbus (1492); the slave trade, the Reformation, smallpox and the conquest (1518); the end of the Ming–Qing wars, the Principia and the Glorious Revolution (1688); coal, the Atlantic economy, fossil fuels and industry (1760); the Russian and American emancipations and the Taiping's end (1862); the end of the slave trade and mass schooling (1870); fertilizer, the war and the flu (1918); and the end of decolonization, Concorde and China's reform (1976). Every process gets a value at each, between its neighbours, unless it already had one there. War and Safety repeat the previous rate, so averages to the next date are conserved; the regional and religious shares still sum to 100.

The gain in world life expectancy is a quantity that adds up: each fall in deaths by cause accounts for some of the years gained, and the parts sum to the whole (a standard demographic decomposition by age and cause). So it is divided by a Cut, whose answers name the Events that are those falls. The deeper causes of each fall (sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics, food, schooling) act together, so they are read by life_cause_record on ev.life-gain instead. The shares are sketched from recalled decompositions: children under five account for close to half of the world's gain, and adult infections for most of the rest before 1970.

changes.value: Changes that add up are divided by Cuts whose answers name what produced them. Each is one decomposition of one change, so it is a Cut on the outcome Event itself rather than a series read across the whole schedule; the series reading recorded a moment ago is replaced by it. (1) The 41.5 years of life expectancy gained since 1900, by the fall in death that produced them, for the whole and for 1900–1950 and 1950–2025, which shows the driver moving from infections toward chronic disease and famine's end; the two halves are weighted by years gained (14 and 27.5), not by duration, and reproduce the whole. (2) The 149 ppm rise in carbon dioxide since 1750, by the emissions that caused it, in proportion to cumulative emissions. (3) The 15 points of land lost from forest since 7900 BCE, by the clearing that removed them. (4) The 6.5 billion people added since 1900, by the region where they were added: a division of where, not why; the why is in the cause readings on ev.population-growth.

The number test asked for the 2025 value of people ever born to be checked against the usual estimate of about 117 billion. The check, recorded in the graph (claude.check.ever-born), finds the 64 billion consistent with this model's own population and life expectancy at every period, and finds that the usual estimate differs almost wholly before 1650, where it assumes a birth rate of about 80 per 1,000, which means a life expectancy near 12.5 years in a population that barely grows. The value stands; its band is widened so both published accounts fall inside it, and it stays tagged exploring until prehistoric life expectancy is checked.

Checked 2026-10-11 against the usual estimate of about 117 billion (Population Reference Bureau). That estimate counts 46 billion births between 8000 BCE and 1 CE and 26 billion between 1 and 1200 by assuming 80 and 60 births per 1,000 a year; in a population that barely grows that means a life expectancy of about 12.5 and 17 years. This model's life expectancy is 25 to 30 in those periods, as palaeodemography and ancient censuses put it, which gives 35 to 40 births per 1,000 and about 22 billion by 1 CE. After 1650 the two accounts agree within a few billion. Raising this value to 117 would contradict the model's own life expectancy before 1650; so it stays, with both accounts inside the band.

An Event's level is judged by how much of humanity it changed and for how long, which is close to how much difference it makes in the cause readings: the top level holds the conditions and transitions on which most later outcomes depend.

upsert.boundary: The Columbian exchange and the collapse of the Americas, 1492 to 1650.
upsert.description: Contact joins the hemispheres. Smallpox, measles and other diseases kill most of the Americas' people, perhaps 50 million falling to under 10; their fields return to forest. American maize, potatoes and cassava later feed growth across Afro-Eurasia.
provenance: inferred: the Americas' 1492 population is contested, from about 8 to over 100 million
upsert.region: The Americas and the Atlantic, joined to Afro-Eurasia

changes.value: The Columbian exchange carries a Cut (the Americas' deaths by cause), so it gets its place: the Americas and the Atlantic, with Afro-Eurasia at the other end. It also names the Americas' share of the world's people, which falls from 11% (1492) to about 2% (1650) across it.

upsert.description: Within History.
Within History.

upsert.boundary: The interwar crisis, October 1929 to September 1939.
upsert.description: The Wall Street crash of 1929 opens a depression that cuts world trade by two thirds and puts a quarter of German and American workers out of work. In Germany it brings the Nazis to power in 1933; in Japan it strengthens the army, which seizes Manchuria in 1931 and invades China in 1937. Italy takes Ethiopia; the League of Nations fails to stop any of them, and Germany rearms, remilitarizes the Rhineland, annexes Austria and dismembers Czechoslovakia.

upsert.boundary: Northern summer sunlight rises with the Earth's orbit, about 23,000 to 11,700 years ago.
upsert.description: As the Earth's tilt and the timing of its closest approach to the Sun shift, summer sunlight at 65° north rises by roughly a tenth to a peak near 11,000 years ago. The ice sheets begin to melt; carbon dioxide released from the Southern Ocean and the loss of reflecting ice amplify the warming. The same cycle ended earlier glacials, Termination II among them.
provenance: inferred: Milankovitch theory and the deglacial chronology, as recalled

changes.value: Causes for two Events at the top of the importance scale that had none: the Holocene and the Second World War. The orbital rise in northern summer sunlight set the deglaciation off; the interwar crisis (the Depression and the regimes it brought to power in Germany and Japan) is what turned the unsettled peace of 1919 into war. The crisis is one Event, not three, so the 1930s do not crowd the schedule; its description names its parts.

The 1930s hold the interwar crisis, antibiotics' beginning and the war's outbreak. Every process gets a value at 1936, the depth of the crisis, between its 1930 and 1940 values, so no curve passes over them. War holds its 1930 rate, so its 1930 to 1939.7 average is conserved; the regional and religious shares still sum to 100.

The Bureau's account has about 47 billion by 1 CE.

Checked 2026-10-11 against the usual estimate of about 117 billion (Population Reference Bureau). That estimate counts 46 billion births between 8000 BCE and 1 CE and 26 billion between 1 and 1200 by assuming 80 and 60 births per 1,000 a year; in a population that barely grows that means a life expectancy of about 12.5 and 17 years. This model's life expectancy is 25 to 30 in those periods, as palaeodemography and ancient censuses put it, which gives 35 to 40 births per 1,000 and about 22 billion by 1 CE. After 1650 the two accounts agree within a few billion. Raising this value to 117 would contradict the model's own life expectancy before 1650; so it stays, with both accounts inside the band.

upsert.reason: Integral of humanity times a crude birth rate consistent with the model's life expectancy; the upper band holds the Population Reference Bureau's account (about 117 billion by 2022).

upsert.boundary: The Earth, followed from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: The Earth as the setting of human history: its orbit and climate, ice and sea level, carbon dioxide and land cover. Two glacial cycles pass in this span, then the Holocene, then the warming people cause. The Events of the Earth itself, its glacials, deglaciations and climate shifts, sit here; what people do to it sits in humanity's history and names the Earth's processes it changes.
provenance: inferred: the lifecycle of the Earth, opened only over this model's span

upsert.boundary: Humanity, followed from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: The history of Homo sapiens as one population: four ages, foragers in Africa, foragers across the world, the agrarian age and the modern age, each opened into eras. The Events that changed humanity as a whole, or several regions at once, sit here; the history of each region sits in that region's own lifecycle.
provenance: inferred: the lifecycle of humanity, opened only over this model's span

upsert.boundary: The history of Africa, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: Homo sapiens' homeland, where the species lived alone for most of its history and from which every other population descends. Its own eras run from the Middle Stone Age through herders, Pharaohs, iron and the Bantu expansion, kingdoms and the trade of the Sahara and the Indian Ocean, the Atlantic era of the slave trade, colonial conquest and rule, to independent Africa, home in 2025 to about a fifth of humanity and most of its growth.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts, such as the UNESCO General History of Africa and the Cambridge History of Africa (sources to check)

upsert.boundary: The history of the Americas, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: No people live in the Americas until the late glacial; they arrive across Beringia, perhaps by 23,000 years ago and certainly by 16,000, and for the next fifteen thousand years the hemisphere's history runs apart from Afro-Eurasia's, inventing farming, cities and states of its own. Contact in 1492 brings epidemics and conquest, colonies built on silver, sugar and slavery, then independent nations, mass immigration and, in the twentieth century, the world's largest economy.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts, such as the Cambridge History of the Native Peoples of the Americas and the Cambridge History of Latin America (sources to check)

upsert.boundary: The history of Antarctica, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: Ice-covered and never inhabited; first sighted in 1820, explored in the heroic age to 1922, reached at the Pole in 1911, and since 1959 held under the Antarctic Treaty for peaceful science.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; sources to check: the Antarctic Treaty Secretariat's history, and Stephen Pyne, The Ice (1986)

upsert.boundary: The history of Asia, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: Home to most of humanity since farming spread, Asia holds the first farmers of south-west Asia, China and South Asia, the first cities and writing, the classical empires of Persia, India and China, the caliphates, the Mongol empire, the gunpowder empires, a century and a half of Western dominance, and since 1945 independence and the largest rise in living standards in history.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts, such as the Cambridge History of China, the New Cambridge History of India and the New Cambridge History of Islam (sources to check)

upsert.boundary: The history of Australia and New Zealand
upsert.description: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples over 50,000 years or more, Māori from about 1280, British colonies from 1788 and 1840, and the dominions and nations since.

upsert.boundary: The history of the Caribbean
upsert.description: Taíno and Kalinago islands, the first landfall of Columbus, the sugar islands of slavery, the Haitian Revolution, and the islands' independence or continued dependence.

upsert.boundary: The history of Central America
upsert.description: Mesoamerica: maize's homeland, the Olmec, Maya, Teotihuacan, Zapotec, Toltec and Aztec worlds, then New Spain, Mexico and the republics of the isthmus.

upsert.boundary: The history of Central Asia
upsert.description: The steppe and the oases: Bactria and Sogdiana, the Silk Road's middle, Turkic and Mongol empires, Timur's Samarkand, Russian conquest and Soviet rule, and independence in 1991.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: UNESCO History of Civilizations of Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: The history of Eastern Africa
upsert.description: The Rift Valley, where many of the oldest Homo sapiens fossils lie, the Ethiopian highlands of Aksum and the Solomonic kingdom, the Swahili coast's trading towns, Great Zimbabwe, Madagascar settled from Borneo, and the colonies and nations from Kenya to Mozambique.

upsert.boundary: The history of Eastern Asia
upsert.description: China, Korea, Japan and Mongolia: millet and rice farming, the Shang and Zhou, the empire of Qin and Han and its successors to the Qing, Korea's and Japan's kingdoms, the Mongols, then the century of humiliation, Japan's empire, the People's Republic and East Asia's rise.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: Cambridge History of China; Cambridge History of Japan)

upsert.boundary: The history of Eastern Europe
upsert.description: The Pontic steppe of the Yamnaya, the Slavs, Kyivan Rus, the Mongol yoke, Poland–Lithuania, Muscovy's growth into the Russian empire across Siberia, serfdom and its end, the Soviet Union and its fall.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: Cambridge History of Russia)

upsert.boundary: The history of Europe, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: Neanderthal country until Homo sapiens arrives about 45,000 years ago, Europe takes farming from south-west Asia and its Bronze Age peoples from the steppe, then builds the Greek and Roman worlds, the Christian kingdoms of the Middle Ages and, from about 1500, the oceanic empires, the scientific and industrial revolutions and the two world wars, before uniting most of its western half in peace after 1945.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts, such as the New Cambridge Medieval History and the Penguin History of Europe (sources to check)

upsert.boundary: The history of Latin America and the Caribbean
upsert.description: Mesoamerica and the Andes, two of the world's independent cradles of farming and states, then Spanish and Portuguese colonies, the Caribbean's sugar and slavery, independence in the 1800s and the nations since.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: Cambridge History of Latin America)

upsert.boundary: The history of Melanesia
upsert.description: New Guinea's highland farmers at Kuk, the Lapita potters of the Bismarcks, the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia and Fiji, labour recruiting, colonies and independence.

upsert.boundary: The history of Micronesia
upsert.description: Islands settled from the Philippines and from Melanesia about 3,500 to 2,000 years ago; Spanish Guam from 1668, then German, Japanese and American rule, the Pacific war and nuclear tests, and the free-association states.

upsert.boundary: The history of Middle Africa
upsert.description: The Congo basin and its rainforest, the Lake Chad basin, the Bantu homeland near the Cameroon–Nigeria border, the Kongo and Lunda kingdoms, Angola's role in the slave trade, the Congo Free State, and the wars of the Congo after 1960.

upsert.boundary: The history of Northern Africa
upsert.description: The Nile valley and the Maghreb: Pharaonic Egypt, Carthage and Roman Africa, the Arab conquest and Islam, the Fatimid, Almoravid, Almohad and Mamluk states, Ottoman rule, French, British and Italian colonies, and independent states from 1922 (Egypt) to 1962 (Algeria).
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: Cambridge History of Africa)

upsert.boundary: The history of Northern America
upsert.description: Clovis hunters, the Archaic and Woodland peoples, the Mississippian towns and Ancestral Puebloans, the Norse in Greenland and Vinland, British and French colonies, the United States and Canada.

upsert.boundary: The history of Northern Europe
upsert.description: The British Isles, Scandinavia and the Baltic: megaliths, the Vikings, Norman England, the Hanseatic towns, Sweden's empire, Britain's parliament, coal and industry, and the Nordic welfare states.

upsert.boundary: The history of Oceania, from 300,000 years ago to 2025
upsert.description: Sahul, the joined Australia and New Guinea, is reached by sea 65,000 or about 50,000 years ago; its peoples keep the longest continuous cultures on Earth. New Guinea invents farming on its own. From about 3,500 years ago Austronesian voyagers settle the remote Pacific, reaching Aotearoa last, about 1280. European contact from 1768 brings epidemics, colonization and settler states, and in the twentieth century the island nations' independence.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts, such as the Cambridge History of the Pacific Islanders and the Cambridge History of Australia (sources to check)

upsert.boundary: The history of Polynesia
upsert.description: Tonga and Samoa settled by Lapita voyagers about 2,850 years ago, then the long pause and the great voyages east to the Society Islands, Hawai'i and Rapa Nui; chiefdoms and kingdoms, missionaries and colonies, and the Pacific nations.

upsert.boundary: The history of South America
upsert.description: Monte Verde, Caral, Chavín, Moche, Nazca, Tiwanaku, Wari, Chimú and the Inca in the Andes, Amazonian societies, Spanish Peru and Portuguese Brazil, independence and the republics.

upsert.boundary: The history of South-eastern Asia
upsert.description: The islands and the mainland: early seafarers on the way to Sahul, Austronesian farmers, Funan, Srivijaya, Angkor, Pagan, Majapahit and Ayutthaya, the spice trade, Dutch, Spanish, British and French colonies, the Vietnam wars and the region's growth.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: Cambridge History of Southeast Asia)

upsert.boundary: The history of Southern Africa
upsert.description: The caves of the Cape coast with the earliest signs of symbolic behaviour, the Khoe and San, Bantu-speaking farmers, Mapungubwe, the Cape Colony, the Zulu kingdom, the mineral revolution, apartheid and its end.

upsert.boundary: The history of Southern Asia
upsert.description: Mehrgarh and the Indus cities, the Vedic age, the Buddha, the Mauryas and Guptas, Persia's empires from Cyrus to the Safavids, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughals, British India, partition and the republics of India, Pakistan and Bangladesh.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: New Cambridge History of India; Cambridge History of Iran)

upsert.boundary: The history of Southern Europe
upsert.description: The Mediterranean peninsulas: Minoan and Mycenaean palaces, Greece and Rome, al-Andalus and the Reconquista, the Italian city-states and the Renaissance, the Iberian empires, and the Balkans under Byzantium, the Ottomans and the nations after them.

upsert.boundary: The history of Sub-Saharan Africa
upsert.description: Africa south of the Sahara: the homeland of most of humanity's genetic diversity, of the Bantu expansion and of the kingdoms of the Sahel, the forest, the Great Lakes and the Zambezi, then of the Atlantic slave trade's victims, colonial rule and the independent states of the twentieth century.
provenance: inferred: standard accounts (sources to check: UNESCO General History of Africa)

upsert.boundary: The history of Western Africa
upsert.description: The Sahel and the forest: Nok's iron and terracottas, the gold empires of Ghana, Mali and Songhay, Ife and Benin, the Atlantic slave trade's coast, Asante, Oyo, Dahomey and Sokoto, British and French colonies, and Nigeria, Africa's most populous state.

upsert.boundary: The history of Western Asia
upsert.description: The Levant and Mesopotamia, where farming, cities, writing and the first empires began; the Hebrew Bible's world, Christianity's and Islam's birthplaces, the caliphates of Damascus and Baghdad, the Ottoman empire, and the states and wars of the twentieth century.

upsert.boundary: The history of Western Europe
upsert.description: Chauvet and Lascaux, the Celts, Roman Gaul, the Franks and Charlemagne, the Holy Roman Empire, France's monarchy and revolution, the Dutch Republic, Germany's unification, the world wars and European union.

changes.value: The Events pass, step 1: the places and categories Events are filed under. Humanity and the Earth become Things with lifecycles of their own inside History, and the Earth's land is opened by the UN M49 standard (2026 borders, used for all times) into six regions, seventeen subregions and the seven intermediate regions of Sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America, each a Thing whose lifecycle is the history of what happens there. The twelve dimensions of a human way of living carved in structure/history-tree.mjs, with the Earth as setting beside them, become concepts, so each Event can say which dimension it belongs to. Importance scales are declared for those who follow each region and each dimension, beside the scale for everyone.

Each process says what it is about. The world measures of people (population, life, food, output, rank, belief, connection, rule and the rest) are about humanity as a whole; temperature, carbon dioxide, sea level and forest are about the Earth; each regional share is about its region. A process about one Thing is then held to that Thing's own Events and to the Events that name it, so the history of Mali or of the Tang does not ask the world's carbon dioxide for a value, while an Event that does change a world measure still names it and is held to it. No value changes.

upsert.boundary: The agrarian age, 9700 BCE to 1750
upsert.description: Farming, invented independently in at least seven regions, spreads until most people are farmers living under states. Numbers grow from a few million to about 790 million while output per person barely rises: the Malthusian condition (MalthusianTrap#0f6b). Writing, cities, empires, the world religions and long-distance trade arise; epidemics, famines and wars set numbers back again and again.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; numbers from this model's own h.humanity
sources to check: Bellwood, First Farmers (2005); Christian, Maps of Time (2004)

upsert.boundary: Foragers in Africa, about 300,000 to 62,000 years ago
upsert.description: For more than three quarters of its history Homo sapiens lives only in Africa, with brief ventures into south-west Asia, in small foraging bands numbering perhaps a few hundred thousand people in all, through two glacial cycles. Bodies become fully modern, and from about 100,000 years ago ochre, shell beads and engraved patterns show a symbolic culture that comes and goes with the size and connection of populations.
provenance: inferred: as recalled from the standard account

sources to check: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546 (Jebel Irhoud); Scerri et al. 2018, Trends in Ecology and Evolution 33 (subdivided populations across Africa); Stringer, The Origin of Our Species (2011)
upsert.region: Africa, with ventures into Western Asia

upsert.boundary: Foragers across the world, about 62,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: From a small population that leaves Africa about 60,000 to 50,000 years ago, Homo sapiens spreads to every continent but Antarctica, absorbing Neanderthals and Denisovans as the archaic humans disappear, while many large animals go extinct where people arrive. Everyone still lives by foraging: perhaps one to a few million people at the Last Glacial Maximum.
provenance: sources to check: Reich, Who We Are and How We Got Here (2018); Bergström et al. 2021, Nature 590 (origins of modern human ancestry)

upsert.boundary: The modern age, 1750 to 2025
upsert.description: Fossil fuels break the agrarian limit: output per person grows faster than population for the first time, life expectancy more than doubles, population grows tenfold to 8.2 billion, and most people come to live in towns, to read and to vote, while bondage ends in law. The same power brings colonial empires, two world wars, nuclear weapons and a warming climate.
provenance: inferred: numbers from this model's own series
sources to check: Our World in Data; Maddison Project Database 2023; McNeill and Pomeranz (eds.), The Cambridge World History, vol. 7 (2015)

upsert.boundary: The classical empires, 500 BCE to 500 CE
upsert.description: Persia, the Mauryas and Guptas, Qin and Han China and Rome each unify a great region; at the turn of the era Rome and Han together rule perhaps half of humanity. The Silk Roads and the monsoon trade join them, and Buddhism and Christianity travel along them. The Antonine plague, the fall of the Han and the end of the western Roman empire close the era.
provenance: sources to check: Scheidel (ed.), Rome and China (2009); Benjamin (ed.), The Cambridge World History, vol. 4 (2015)
upsert.region: Europe, Western, Southern and Eastern Asia, and Northern Africa

upsert.boundary: The Cold War and decolonization, 1945 to 1991
upsert.description: The United States and the Soviet Union divide the world without fighting each other directly; almost every colony becomes a state; vaccines, antibiotics and the green revolution lift world life expectancy from 46 to about 64 years and population doubles; Japan and then East Asia's tigers grow fast; the jet, the computer and the satellite arrive. The era ends with the Soviet Union's dissolution.
provenance: inferred: numbers from this model's own series
sources to check: Westad, The Global Cold War (2005); Leffler and Westad (eds.), The Cambridge History of the Cold War (2010)

upsert.boundary: The dispersal and the Upper Palaeolithic, about 62,000 to 26,000 years ago
upsert.description: People cross into Asia, reach Sahul by sea and spread through Europe from about 45,000 years ago; the Neanderthals vanish about 40,000 years ago. Figurative art appears in Sulawesi and in Europe, with needles, the spear-thrower, burials with grave goods and exchange networks hundreds of kilometres long.
provenance: sources to check: Higham et al. 2014, Nature 512 (Neanderthal disappearance); Aubert et al. 2019, Nature 576 (Sulawesi art)

upsert.boundary: The early modern world, 1450 to 1750
upsert.description: European ships join the hemispheres and round Africa to Asia; the Columbian exchange moves crops, animals and diseases, the Americas' peoples collapse and enslaved Africans are shipped to their plantations; silver from Potosí flows to China. Gunpowder empires (Ottoman, Safavid, Mughal, Ming and Qing, Russia) rule most of Eurasia, while printing, the Reformation and the scientific revolution change Europe.
provenance: sources to check: Bentley, Subrahmanyam and Wiesner-Hanks (eds.), The Cambridge World History, vol. 6 (2015)

upsert.boundary: The first Homo sapiens, about 300,000 to 132,000 years ago
upsert.description: Fossils with modern faces and older braincases at Jebel Irhoud (about 315,000 years), Florisbad (about 260,000) and Omo Kibish (about 230,000) show a species forming across Africa from connected populations rather than in one cradle. People make Middle Stone Age points and flakes and use fire. The penultimate glacial, from about 190,000 years ago, is long and cold.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; fossil ages contested by tens of thousands of years
sources to check: Hublin et al. 2017, Nature 546; Vidal et al. 2022, Nature 601 (Omo Kibish)

upsert.boundary: The first farmers, 9700 to 3500 BCE
upsert.description: Wheat, barley, sheep and goats in south-west Asia, millet and rice in China, squash and maize in Mesoamerica, taro and bananas in New Guinea, and later crops in the Andes and Africa; farming peoples expand into Europe, South Asia and East Asia and replace or absorb foragers. Villages grow into towns such as Çatalhöyük; copper is smelted; by the era's end irrigation farmers crowd the Mesopotamian plain.
provenance: sources to check: Bellwood, First Farmers (2005); Larson et al. 2014, PNAS 111 (domestication)
upsert.region: Western, Eastern and Southern Asia, Europe, the Americas, Melanesia and Africa

upsert.boundary: The first states, 3500 to 1200 BCE
upsert.description: Cities, kings, taxes and writing in Mesopotamia and Egypt, then the Indus valley, China's Shang and the palaces of Crete and Mycenae; bronze, the wheel, the plough, the domesticated horse and the chariot; the first written law codes. Herding peoples from the Pontic steppe carry their languages across Europe and into South Asia. The era ends in the collapse of the eastern Mediterranean's Bronze Age states.
provenance: sources to check: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (3rd ed. 2016); Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007)
upsert.region: Western and Southern Asia, Northern Africa, Eastern Asia and Europe

upsert.boundary: The glacial maximum and the peopling of the Americas, about 26,000 to 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets at their greatest drive people from the far north into refugia. Dogs are domesticated, pottery appears in East Asia, and people enter the Americas. As the world warms after about 19,000 years ago, the Natufians of the Levant settle in villages and harvest wild cereals; the Younger Dryas cold closes the age.
provenance: sources to check: Clark et al. 2009, Science 325 (the Last Glacial Maximum); Wu et al. 2012, Science 336 (Xianrendong pottery)

upsert.boundary: The globalized world, 1991 to 2025
upsert.description: One world market, the internet and the mobile phone; China's and India's growth lift about a billion people out of extreme poverty; fertility falls below replacement in most countries; democracy spreads, then recedes; financial crisis, terrorism and the wars in Iraq, Syria and Ukraine; COVID-19; warming passes 1.4 °C.
provenance: inferred: numbers from this model's own series
sources to check: World Bank, Poverty and Shared Prosperity reports; UN World Population Prospects 2024; V-Dem Democracy Report 2025

upsert.boundary: Iron and the first empires, 1200 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Cheap iron spreads after the Bronze Age collapse and alphabets spread from Phoenicia. Assyria, then Babylon and Persia, build empires that rule many peoples; Zhou China, Vedic India and the Greek city-states take shape; coins are struck in Lydia; in the Americas the Olmec and Chavín flourish. The Axial age's teachers begin to appear.
provenance: sources to check: Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014); Morris, Why the West Rules—for Now (2010)
upsert.region: Western, Southern and Eastern Asia, Europe, Northern Africa and the Americas

upsert.boundary: The Last Interglacial and its aftermath, about 132,000 to 62,000 years ago
upsert.description: A green Sahara and Arabia open corridors: Homo sapiens reaches the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and perhaps Arabia and beyond, but those groups leave few descendants. In southern Africa coastal groups make engraved ochre and shell beads (Blombos, about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay and Howiesons Poort toolkits. As the glacial returns after about 71,000 years ago, populations shrink and fragment.
provenance: sources to check: Henshilwood et al. 2002, Science 295 (Blombos engravings); Groucutt et al. 2015, Evolutionary Anthropology 24 (routes out of Africa)

upsert.boundary: The postclassical world, 500 to 1450
upsert.description: Islam arises and its caliphates span Iberia to Central Asia; Tang and Song China lead the world in output, printing and gunpowder; Christian kingdoms form across Europe; states and trade spread through Africa, South-east Asia and the Americas. The Mongols build the largest land empire, and the Black Death, carried along its routes, kills perhaps a third of western Eurasia's people.
provenance: sources to check: Kedar and Wiesner-Hanks (eds.), The Cambridge World History, vol. 5 (2015)

upsert.boundary: Revolutions, industry and empire, 1750 to 1914
upsert.description: The industrial revolution spreads from Britain to Europe, North America and Japan; the American, French, Haitian and Latin American revolutions; steam, rail and the telegraph shrink the world; slavery and serfdom are abolished in law; Europeans conquer most of Africa and South-east Asia; some fifty million Europeans emigrate; the first globalization joins the world's markets.
provenance: sources to check: Bayly, The Birth of the Modern World 1780–1914 (2004); Osterhammel, The Transformation of the World (2014)

upsert.boundary: The world wars, 1914 to 1945
upsert.description: Two world wars and the 1918 influenza kill well over a hundred million people; the Russian, Ottoman, Austrian and German empires fall; communist, fascist and nationalist regimes rise; the first globalization collapses in the Depression. Synthetic fertilizer, vaccines and antibiotics arrive, and the war ends with nuclear weapons.
provenance: sources to check: Hobsbawm, The Age of Extremes (1994); Tooze, The Deluge (2014)

value: exploring: a periodization is a lens chosen for a question, not a fact of time (structure/history-tree.mjs, rejected 'Periods'); these follow the boundaries of common world-history schemes, chosen so that most existing Events fall wholly inside one era

changes.value: The Events pass, step 2: the long run first. Humanity's history is opened into four ages (foragers in Africa, foragers across the world, the agrarian age, the modern age) and those into twelve eras that partition it in time, so an era's Events are in place before the smaller ones inside them. The existing world-scale Events move from History into the age or era that contains their whole interval; those that straddle two stay in the age or in humanity's history; smallpox in the Americas becomes part of the Columbian exchange and the COVID vaccines part of the pandemic. The Earth's own Events (glacials, deglaciation, the Holocene, the Little Ice Age, the rise in carbon dioxide, warming and the loss of forest) move into the Earth's lifecycle. Regional Events wait for their regions' own eras.
