upsert.boundary: Alexander's conquests, 334 to 323 BCE
upsert.description: Alexander of Macedon conquers the Persian empire from Egypt to the Indus in eleven years; after his death his generals divide it, and Greek kingdoms rule Egypt, Syria, Mesopotamia and Bactria for centuries, spreading Greek cities, language and art as far as Gandhara.
provenance: sources to check: Bosworth, Conquest and Empire (1988)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Greece, Macedonia); Asia (Western, Southern and Central Asia); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

upsert.boundary: The Achaemenid Persian empire, 550 to 330 BCE
upsert.description: Cyrus conquers the Medes, Lydia and Babylon, freeing the exiled Jews; Darius rules from the Indus to Egypt and Thrace through satraps, a royal road and a standard coinage, the largest empire yet, holding a large share of humanity. Alexander destroys it.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its share of the world's people is uncertain, from perhaps a sixth to over a third
sources to check: Briant, From Cyrus to Alexander (2002)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (Iran, Afghanistan), Western Asia, Central Asia; Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt); Europe (Southern Europe: Thrace)

upsert.boundary: Sargon's empire of Akkad, about 2334 to 2154 BCE
upsert.description: Sargon of Akkad conquers the Sumerian cities and rules from the Gulf to Syria, the first empire over many city-states, with Akkadian as the language of rule; it falls amid revolts, invasion and perhaps drought.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates on the middle chronology
sources to check: Westenholz, in Mesopotamien: Akkade-Zeit und Ur III-Zeit (1999)

upsert.boundary: Ashoka's rule and his edicts of dhamma, about 268 to 232 BCE
upsert.description: Horrified by the slaughter of his war on Kalinga, Ashoka proclaims on rock and pillar edicts a policy of non-violence, tolerance and care for people and animals, and sends Buddhist missions to Sri Lanka and beyond, turning a South Asian sect toward a world religion.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (3rd ed. 2012)

upsert.boundary: The Neo-Assyrian empire, 911 to 609 BCE
upsert.description: From Assur and Nineveh, kings with iron-armed professional armies conquer from Iran to Egypt and deport whole peoples to break resistance; Ashurbanipal gathers a great library; Babylon and the Medes destroy Nineveh in 612 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Radner, Ancient Assyria (2015)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq, Syria); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, briefly)

upsert.boundary: Buddhism spreads to China, Korea and Japan, about 65 to 600
upsert.description: Merchants and monks carry Buddhism along the Silk Roads and the sea routes; after the Han fall it wins converts at every level of Chinese society; Korea's kingdoms adopt it in the 300s and 500s and Japan in 538 or 552; by 600 it is the largest tradition of East Asia's courts and monasteries.
provenance: sources to check: Zürcher, The Buddhist Conquest of China (1959)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Korea, Japan), Central Asia

upsert.boundary: Çatalhöyük, about 7100 to 5950 BCE
upsert.description: A town of perhaps 5,000 people on the Konya plain, with houses entered through the roof, wall paintings and burials under the floors, and no streets or public buildings: a large settlement without visible rulers.
provenance: sources to check: Hodder, The Leopard's Tale (2006)

upsert.boundary: Millet farming in north China, about 8000 to 6000 BCE
upsert.description: Along the Yellow River people domesticate foxtail and broomcorn millet and pigs; villages such as Cishan store millet in pits by about 6000 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Lu et al. 2009, PNAS 106

upsert.boundary: The place-value decimal system with zero, about 499 to 628
upsert.description: Indian mathematicians use nine digits and a zero in a place-value system; Aryabhata (499) computes with it and Brahmagupta (628) gives rules for zero and negative numbers. Through Baghdad's al-Khwarizmi it reaches Europe as 'Arabic numerals'.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the earliest dated zero is debated (the Bakhshali manuscript)
sources to check: Plofker, Mathematics in India (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Denisovans across eastern Asia, about 200,000 to 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: Known from a finger bone and teeth in Denisova Cave in the Altai, a jaw on the Tibetan plateau and a few other bones, and above all from their genome, this archaic population mixed with the ancestors of Melanesians and East Asians; Tibetans carry a Denisovan gene for living at altitude.
provenance: sources to check: Reich et al. 2010, Nature 468; Chen et al. 2019, Nature 569 (Xiahe jaw); Huerta-Sánchez et al. 2014, Nature 512
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern, Central and South-eastern Asia; Europe (Eastern Europe: the Altai in Siberia)

upsert.boundary: Wheat, barley, sheep, goats and cattle domesticated in the Fertile Crescent, about 9500 to 7000 BCE
upsert.description: Over two thousand years, people from the Levant to the Zagros cultivate einkorn, emmer, barley, lentils, peas and flax until they change into domestic forms, and herd sheep, goats, cattle and pigs: the founder crops and animals of south-west Asian farming.
provenance: sources to check: Zeder 2011, Current Anthropology 52; Fuller et al. 2011, Proceedings of the Royal Society B

upsert.boundary: The first pottery, in China and Japan, about 20,000 to 14,000 years ago
upsert.description: Foragers at Xianrendong in south China make clay pots about 20,000 years ago, and people in Japan and the Russian Far East soon after, long before farming: cooking vessels for shellfish, nuts and soups during the cold of the glacial maximum.
provenance: sources to check: Wu et al. 2012, Science 336

upsert.boundary: Göbekli Tepe, about 9500 to 8000 BCE
upsert.description: On a hill in south-east Anatolia, people at the very start of farming raise rings of T-shaped limestone pillars carved with foxes, boars, vultures and snakes, perhaps the oldest monumental ritual site known.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; whether it was a temple or a settlement is debated
sources to check: Schmidt, Göbekli Tepe (2012); Clare et al. 2019, Antiquity 93

upsert.boundary: The Gupta age, about 320 to 550
upsert.description: The Guptas rule north India in an age remembered as classical: Sanskrit drama and poetry (Kālidāsa), the temples and sculpture of Hinduism's devotional cults, the university at Nalanda, and Aryabhata's astronomy; Hun invasions bring it down.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Early India (2002)

upsert.boundary: Hammurabi's Babylon, about 1792 to 1750 BCE
upsert.description: Hammurabi unites Mesopotamia from Babylon and has nearly three hundred laws carved on a stele, with penalties graded by the rank of the victim: the best-known of the early law codes.
provenance: sources to check: Roth, Law Collections from Mesopotamia and Asia Minor (1995)

upsert.boundary: The Han dynasty, 206 BCE to 220 CE
upsert.description: The Han keep Qin's centralized empire but govern it through Confucian-trained officials; the census of 2 CE counts about 58 million people. Han armies push into Central Asia and open the Silk Roads; paper is invented; the dynasty falls apart in rebellion and warlordism after 184.
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (2007); Loewe, in The Cambridge History of China vol. 1 (1986)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China), Central Asia, South-eastern Asia (northern Vietnam)

upsert.boundary: The Hittite kingdom, about 1650 to 1180 BCE
upsert.description: From Hattusa in central Anatolia, the Hittites rule an empire that rivals Egypt, sacks Babylon (1595 BCE), fights Ramesses II at Kadesh and writes the earliest recorded Indo-European language, until the Bronze Age collapse.
provenance: sources to check: Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (2nd ed. 2005)

upsert.boundary: Confucius and the Hundred Schools of Thought, 551 to 221 BCE
upsert.description: In an age of warring states, Confucius teaches ritual, filial duty and government by virtue; Laozi and Zhuangzi the way of nature; Mozi universal care; Mencius and Xunzi argue over human nature; the Legalists, law and punishment. Confucian and Daoist traditions shape China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for two thousand years.
provenance: sources to check: Graham, Disputers of the Tao (1989)

upsert.boundary: The Indus civilization, about 2600 to 1900 BCE
upsert.description: Planned cities of baked brick, Mohenjo-daro and Harappa among them, with drains, granaries and standard weights, spread over a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia together; their script is still undeciphered; the cities decline after 1900 BCE as rivers shift and monsoons weaken.
provenance: sources to check: Wright, The Ancient Indus (2010); Giosan et al. 2012, PNAS 109

upsert.boundary: Israel and Judah, the exile and the Hebrew Bible, about 1000 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: Small kingdoms in the hills of Canaan worship Yahweh; Assyria destroys Israel (722 BCE) and Babylon destroys Jerusalem and exiles Judah's elite (587 BCE); in exile and after the return under Persia, scribes shape the Hebrew Bible and a strict monotheism that Christianity and Islam later inherit.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the dating of the biblical texts is debated
sources to check: Finkelstein and Silberman, The Bible Unearthed (2001)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Israel, Palestine; Iraq for Babylon)

upsert.boundary: The Jōmon of Japan, about 14,500 to 300 BCE
upsert.description: Settled foragers who fish, gather nuts and make cord-marked pottery live in villages across Japan for more than ten thousand years, among the most enduring foraging societies known, until Yayoi rice farmers arrive from Korea.
provenance: sources to check: Habu, Ancient Jomon of Japan (2004)

upsert.boundary: Early states in Korea and Japan, about 57 BCE to 668
upsert.description: Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla compete on the Korean peninsula until Silla, allied with Tang China, unifies it (668); in Japan, Yayoi rice farmers from Korea are followed by the great keyhole tombs of the Kofun period and the Yamato state, which adopts Chinese writing and Buddhism.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the founding dates of the Korean kingdoms are traditional
sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010); Farris, Sacred Texts and Buried Treasures (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Kushan empire, about 30 to 375
upsert.description: Rulers from Central Asia hold Bactria and north India, trade with Rome, Parthia and Han China, patronize Buddhism and the Gandhara art that first shows the Buddha in human form, often in Greek style.
provenance: sources to check: Liu, The Silk Road in World History (2010)
upsert.region: Asia: Central Asia, Southern Asia (Afghanistan, Pakistan, India)

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens in the Levant: Misliya, Skhul and Qafzeh, about 180,000 to 90,000 years ago
upsert.description: A jaw at Misliya Cave (about 180,000 years old) and burials at Skhul and Qafzeh (about 120,000 to 90,000) show Homo sapiens in south-west Asia long before the main dispersal; these groups, living beside Neanderthals, leave few or no descendants among people alive today.
provenance: sources to check: Hershkovitz et al. 2018, Science 359; Grun et al. 2005, Journal of Human Evolution 49

upsert.boundary: The Maurya empire, 321 to 185 BCE
upsert.description: Chandragupta Maurya, said to be advised by Kautilya, author of the Arthashastra, builds the first empire over most of the subcontinent from Pataliputra; his grandson Ashoka extends it to all but the far south.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Aśoka and the Decline of the Mauryas (3rd ed. 2012)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Bangladesh)

upsert.boundary: Mehrgarh, about 7000 to 2600 BCE
upsert.description: At the foot of the Bolan pass in Baluchistan, villagers farm wheat and barley and herd cattle, sheep and goats, drill teeth and make beads: the roots of farming in South Asia and of the Indus cities.
provenance: sources to check: Jarrige 2008, Pragdhara 18; Coppa et al. 2006, Nature 440

upsert.boundary: Paper made in China, about 150 BCE to 105 CE
upsert.description: Paper from hemp and rags appears in China in the second century BCE; the court official Cai Lun improves it about 105 CE with bark and fishnet. It reaches Samarkand by the 700s, Baghdad by about 800 and Europe by the 1100s, and makes books cheap enough for printing to matter.
provenance: sources to check: Tsien, Paper and Printing, in Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)

upsert.boundary: The Parthian empire, 247 BCE to 224 CE
upsert.description: Iranian horse archers from the north-east take over the Seleucid lands from the Euphrates to the Indus, stop Rome at Carrhae (53 BCE) and control the Silk Road's middle.
provenance: sources to check: Curtis and Stewart (eds.), The Age of the Parthians (2007)

upsert.boundary: Qin unifies China, 221 to 206 BCE
upsert.description: The First Emperor conquers the last of the warring states and imposes one script, one coinage, standard weights, axle widths and laws, ruled through appointed officials in commanderies rather than nobles; the dynasty falls soon after his death, but the unified empire endures.
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Sasanian empire, 224 to 651
upsert.description: A Persian dynasty restores Iranian rule from Mesopotamia to Central Asia with Zoroastrianism as its state religion, fights Rome and Byzantium for four centuries, and is destroyed by the Arab conquest after its last great war with Byzantium (602 to 628) leaves both exhausted.
provenance: sources to check: Daryaee, Sasanian Persia (2009)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (Iran), Western Asia (Iraq), Central Asia

upsert.boundary: The Shang dynasty, about 1600 to 1046 BCE
upsert.description: Kings at Anyang cast great bronze ritual vessels, drive chariots and consult their ancestors on cracked bones and shells, whose inscriptions (from about 1250 BCE) are the oldest Chinese writing.
provenance: sources to check: Keightley, The Ancestral Landscape (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Buddha and Mahavira, about 500 to 400 BCE
upsert.description: In the cities of the Ganges plain, the Buddha teaches the end of suffering through the middle way and the eightfold path, and Mahavira the non-violence of Jainism; both found orders of monks and nuns that reject the authority of the Vedas and the priests.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Buddha's dates vary by about a century
sources to check: Gethin, The Foundations of Buddhism (1998)

upsert.boundary: The Sui reunify China, 581 to 618
upsert.description: After nearly four centuries of division, the Sui reunite north and south (589), dig the Grand Canal joining the Yangtze to the Yellow River, and bring back the examination of officials, but exhaust the country in wars with Goguryeo and fall to the Tang.
provenance: sources to check: Wright, The Sui Dynasty (1978)

upsert.boundary: Cave paintings in Sulawesi and Borneo, about 45,000 to 40,000 years ago
upsert.description: Painted pigs, buffalo and hand stencils in limestone caves of Sulawesi and Borneo, dated by uranium in the crusts over them, are among the oldest figurative art known, older than Europe's Chauvet.
provenance: sources to check: Aubert et al. 2014, Nature 514; Brumm et al. 2021, Science Advances 7

upsert.boundary: The Sumerian city-states, about 2900 to 2350 BCE
upsert.description: Ur, Uruk, Lagash, Kish and a dozen other cities, each under its god and king, fight over water and fields; the royal tombs of Ur hold gold, lyres and sacrificed attendants; the stories of Gilgamesh begin here.
provenance: sources to check: Van De Mieroop, A History of the Ancient Near East (3rd ed. 2016)

upsert.boundary: The Upanishads, about 800 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Teachers in the Ganges plain turn from sacrifice to the self: atman is brahman, and the soul passes through rebirths according to its karma until it is freed. These ideas underlie later Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism.

upsert.boundary: Uruk, the first city, about 3500 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: On the lower Euphrates, Uruk grows to perhaps 40,000 people or more, with monumental temples, mass-produced ration bowls, cylinder seals, colonies up the river, and the first written accounts.
provenance: sources to check: Algaze, Ancient Mesopotamia at the Dawn of Civilization (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Vedic age in north India, about 1500 to 600 BCE
upsert.description: Speakers of Indo-Aryan languages, carrying steppe ancestry, settle the Punjab and then the Ganges plain; their priests compose the Rigveda and later Vedas, the varna order of priests, warriors, traders and servants takes shape, and iron opens the Ganges forests to farming.
provenance: sources to check: Thapar, Early India (2002); Narasimhan et al. 2019, Science 365

upsert.boundary: The Warring States, 475 to 221 BCE
upsert.description: Seven Chinese states fight with mass infantry, crossbows and iron, and reform to survive: land registers, salaried officials, written law. War eliminates the states that raise and organize less, and Qin, reformed under Shang Yang, absorbs the rest (Warsift#b01b).
provenance: sources to check: Lewis, Sanctioned Violence in Early China (1990); Hui, War and State Formation in Ancient China and Early Modern Europe (2005)

upsert.boundary: Rice domesticated in the Yangtze valley, about 7000 to 5000 BCE
upsert.description: People of the lower Yangtze, at sites such as Shangshan and Hemudu, gather and then cultivate wild rice until it no longer sheds its grain, over two thousand years; rice later feeds the densest farming populations on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Fuller et al. 2009, Science 323

upsert.boundary: The Zhou overthrow the Shang, 1046 BCE
upsert.description: At Muye the Zhou defeat the last Shang king and justify it by the Mandate of Heaven, the idea that heaven grants rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from the wicked, which every later Chinese dynasty invokes.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the date follows the Xia–Shang–Zhou Chronology Project
sources to check: Shaughnessy, in The Cambridge History of Ancient China (1999)

upsert.boundary: Zoroastrianism, about 1000 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: The hymns attributed to Zarathustra teach a struggle between truth and the lie under one wise lord, Ahura Mazda, with a judgment after death; under the Achaemenids and later the Sasanians it becomes the religion of Iran's rulers and shapes Jewish, Christian and Muslim ideas of heaven, hell and the end of time.
provenance: exploring: Zarathustra's date is placed anywhere from about 1500 to 500 BCE

upsert.boundary: The Axial age, about 800 to 200 BCE
upsert.description: In China, India, Iran, Israel and Greece, within a few centuries and largely apart, teachers and writers turn from ritual and myth toward ethics, the inner life and argued philosophy: the Upanishads, the Buddha and Mahavira, Confucius and Laozi, the prophets of Israel, and the Greek philosophers. Most of the world's major traditions of thought still trace back to them.
provenance: exploring: whether the Axial age is one phenomenon, as Jaspers argued, is debated
sources to check: Jaspers, The Origin and Goal of History (1953); Bellah and Joas (eds.), The Axial Age and Its Consequences (2012)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern, Southern and Western Asia); Europe (Southern Europe: Greece)

upsert.boundary: The Bronze Age collapse, about 1200 to 1150 BCE
upsert.description: Within a few decades the palaces of Mycenaean Greece, the Hittite empire and cities of the Levant such as Ugarit are destroyed and abandoned; Egypt fights off the 'Sea Peoples' but declines; writing disappears in Greece for four centuries. Drought, earthquakes, raiders and the breakdown of the trade that brought tin are all blamed.
provenance: sources to check: Cline, 1177 B.C. (2014); Kaniewski et al. 2013, PLoS ONE 8
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia); Europe (Southern Europe: Greece); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

upsert.boundary: Horses tamed for riding and the war chariot, about 2200 to 1500 BCE
upsert.description: The modern domestic horse is bred on the steppe north of the Caucasus about 2200 BCE and spreads across Eurasia within a few centuries; the light spoked-wheel chariot, first found in Sintashta graves east of the Urals, becomes the weapon of elites from Egypt to China.
provenance: sources to check: Librado et al. 2021, Nature 598; Anthony, The Horse, the Wheel, and Language (2007)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: the Pontic–Volga steppe and the Urals); Asia (Central, Western, Southern and Eastern Asia)

upsert.boundary: Copper smelted, then bronze, about 5000 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Smelting copper from ore begins in the Balkans and Iran by about 5000 BCE; arsenical and then tin bronze follows in south-west Asia, giving harder tools and weapons and a trade in metal and tin across thousands of kilometres.
provenance: sources to check: Radivojević et al. 2010, Journal of Archaeological Science 37; Roberts, Thornton and Pigott 2009, Antiquity 83
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Asia (Western and Southern Asia)

upsert.boundary: The Silk Roads, about 130 BCE to 1450
upsert.description: After Zhang Qian's missions to Central Asia, chains of caravan routes and oasis cities join China, Central Asia, Iran, India and the Mediterranean; silk, horses, glass, paper, spices and silver travel along them, and so do Buddhism, Christianity, Manichaeism and Islam, and the plague.
provenance: sources to check: Hansen, The Silk Road: A New History (2012); Frankopan, The Silk Roads (2015)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern, Central, Southern and Western Asia); Europe; Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Toba super-eruption, about 74,000 years ago
upsert.description: A volcano in Sumatra erupts, the largest eruption of the last two million years, spreading ash across South Asia and cooling the climate for some years; whether it nearly wiped out humanity, as once argued, is doubted, since tool-makers in India and Africa carry on through it.
provenance: exploring: the eruption's effect on people is contested
sources to check: Petraglia et al. 2007, Science 317; Smith et al. 2018, Nature 555

upsert.boundary: Writing invented in Mesopotamia and Egypt, about 3300 to 3100 BCE
upsert.description: Uruk's administrators turn counting tokens into signs pressed in clay tablets to record grain, animals and labour; within a few centuries the signs also write sounds, and cuneiform carries laws, letters and literature. Egypt's hieroglyphs appear at about the same time, perhaps independently. Writing is later invented again in China and Mesoamerica.
provenance: sources to check: Schmandt-Besserat, Before Writing (1992); Woods (ed.), Visible Language (2010)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Mesopotamia); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

changes.value: Asia's own history to 600, inside its eras: early Homo sapiens in the Levant, the Denisovans and the Toba eruption; cave art in Sulawesi, the first pottery, the Jōmon; Göbekli Tepe, the Fertile Crescent's domestications, Çatalhöyük, millet and rice in China, Mehrgarh; Uruk, the Sumerian city-states, Akkad, the Indus cities, Hammurabi, the Hittites, the Shang and the Vedic age; Israel and the Hebrew Bible, Zoroastrianism, Assyria, the Achaemenid empire, the Upanishads, the Buddha and Mahavira, Confucius and the Hundred Schools, the Warring States; the Mauryas and Ashoka, Qin and Han, paper, the Kushans, Buddhism's arrival in China, the Sasanians, the Guptas, the place-value decimal with zero, Korea's and Japan's early states and the Sui. With them come seven world Events in humanity's eras: writing, metallurgy, the horse and the chariot, the Bronze Age collapse, the Axial age, Alexander's conquests and the Silk Roads. Events that turn a world measure name it: writing (literacy), the Axial age and its traditions and the spread of Buddhism (the shares of religious traditions), the Achaemenid, Qin and Han states (the largest polity's share of humanity).

The conquest of North Africa, part of the Arab conquests.

upsert.description: The Mongols conquer the Southern Song by 1279.

upsert.boundary: The Abbasid caliphate, 750 to 1258
upsert.description: A revolution based in Khurasan overthrows the Umayyads; the Abbasids build Baghdad (762), which grows to perhaps half a million people or more, among the largest cities in the world. Their real power fades after the 900s, as Buyid and then Seljuk sultans rule in their name, until the Mongols sack Baghdad in 1258.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Baghdad's population is an estimate
sources to check: Kennedy, When Baghdad Ruled the Muslim World (2004)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq, Syria, Arabia), Southern Asia (Iran); Africa (Northern Africa, until the 900s)

upsert.boundary: The An Lushan rebellion, 755 to 763
upsert.description: A frontier general of Sogdian and Turkic descent rebels and takes both Tang capitals; the war and its famines cut the registered population from about 53 million to 17 million, though much of that fall is people lost to the census rather than dead. The Tang survive but lose Central Asia and control of the provinces.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is much disputed
sources to check: Twitchett (ed.), The Cambridge History of China vol. 3 (1979)

upsert.boundary: The Khmer empire of Angkor, 802 to 1431
upsert.description: Jayavarman II proclaims himself universal king in 802; from Angkor his successors rule much of mainland South-east Asia and build Angkor Wat (early 1100s) and the Bayon, in a low-density city of perhaps 750,000 people spread over a vast network of reservoirs and canals. Droughts and floods in the 1300s and 1400s strain its water system, and the court moves south after Ayutthaya's attack.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Angkor's population is an estimate
sources to check: Coe, Angkor and the Khmer Civilization (2003); Buckley et al. 2010, PNAS 107
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Cambodia, Thailand, Laos, Vietnam)

upsert.boundary: The Mongols sack Baghdad, February 1258
upsert.description: Hulagu's army takes Baghdad, kills the last Abbasid caliph and a great part of the city's people, ending the caliphate that had reigned there for five centuries.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is unknown
sources to check: Jackson, The Mongols and the Islamic World (2017)

upsert.boundary: The Chola empire, 848 to 1279
upsert.description: From the Kaveri delta, the Cholas rule South India and Sri Lanka, build the great temple at Thanjavur (1010) and send a fleet against Srivijaya (1025), the largest naval expedition of India's history; Tamil merchant guilds trade from the Gulf to China.
provenance: sources to check: Kulke, Kesavapany and Sakhuja (eds.), Nagapattinam to Suvarnadwipa (2009)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Sri Lanka); South-eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The East India Company takes Bengal, 1757 to 1765
upsert.description: At Plassey (June 1757) Robert Clive's small army, helped by the treachery of the nawab's commander, defeats Siraj ud-Daulah; after victory at Buxar (1764), the Mughal emperor grants the Company the diwani, the right to collect Bengal's revenue (1765). A trading company becomes a territorial ruler, and the Bengal famine of 1770 follows.
provenance: sources to check: Marshall, Bengal: The British Bridgehead (1987); Dalrymple, The Anarchy (2019)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Bangladesh: Bengal); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: The Delhi Sultanate, 1206 to 1526
upsert.description: Turkic and Afghan dynasties rule north India from Delhi, hold off the Mongols and under Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughluq reach far south; Persian becomes the language of rule, Sufi orders spread Islam, and the Qutb Minar rises over Delhi. Timur's sack of Delhi (1398) breaks its power.
provenance: sources to check: Jackson, The Delhi Sultanate (1999)

upsert.boundary: King Sejong's Hangul alphabet, 1443 to 1446
upsert.description: Sejong and his scholars design an alphabet of 28 letters whose shapes follow the organs of speech, published in 1446 so that ordinary people could read and write; the elite keep writing in Chinese characters for centuries, and Hangul becomes the national script only in the 1900s.
provenance: sources to check: Kim-Renaud (ed.), The Korean Alphabet (1997)

upsert.boundary: Heian Japan, 794 to 1185
upsert.description: From Heian-kyō (Kyoto), a court aristocracy dominated by the Fujiwara develops the kana scripts and a literature written largely by women, above all Murasaki Shikibu's Tale of Genji (about 1008), while warrior clans grow in the provinces until the Genpei War (1180 to 1185).
provenance: sources to check: Morris, The World of the Shining Prince (1964)

upsert.boundary: The translation movement and the House of Wisdom, about 770 to 1000
upsert.description: Under Abbasid patronage, Greek, Persian and Indian works of philosophy, medicine, astronomy and mathematics are translated into Arabic; al-Khwarizmi writes on algebra and on the Indian numerals, and scholars from al-Kindi to al-Razi and al-Biruni build on them. Paper mills in Baghdad make books cheaper.
provenance: sources to check: Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq), Southern Asia (Iran), Central Asia

upsert.boundary: Japan's invasions of Korea, 1592 to 1598
upsert.description: Hideyoshi's armies overrun Korea; Admiral Yi Sun-sin's armoured turtle ships cut their supply lines at sea, Ming China sends armies, and the Japanese withdraw after Hideyoshi's death, leaving Korea devastated.
provenance: sources to check: Swope, A Dragon's Head and a Serpent's Tail (2009)

upsert.boundary: Islam spreads in maritime South-east Asia, about 1290 to 1650
upsert.description: Through traders and Sufi teachers from Gujarat, Arabia and Bengal, the rulers of Samudra-Pasai in Sumatra (by the 1290s), then Malacca (early 1400s) and the ports of Java, the Moluccas and Mindanao convert; by the 1600s most people of the Malay world and Java are Muslim, which makes Indonesia today the country with the most Muslims.
provenance: sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008); Reid, Southeast Asia in the Age of Commerce (1988 to 1993)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia, Malaysia, Brunei, the southern Philippines)

upsert.boundary: Japan's unification, 1568 to 1603
upsert.description: After a century of civil war, Oda Nobunaga uses massed musketeers to take Kyoto (1568) and beat the Takeda at Nagashino (1575); Toyotomi Hideyoshi unites the country (1590), disarms the peasants and invades Korea; Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara (1600) and becomes shogun in 1603.

upsert.boundary: Joseon Korea, 1392 to 1897
upsert.description: General Yi Seong-gye founds a dynasty that rules Korea for five centuries as a Neo-Confucian state with examinations and a hereditary yangban elite; King Sejong's scholars create the Hangul alphabet; Japan invades (1592 to 1598) and the Manchus (1627, 1636), and Korea then keeps out most outsiders until the 1870s.
provenance: sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

upsert.boundary: The Kamakura shogunate, 1185 to 1333
upsert.description: After the Genpei War, Minamoto no Yoritomo founds a warrior government at Kamakura beside the imperial court; the samurai become Japan's rulers, Zen and Pure Land Buddhism spread, and the shogunate repels two Mongol invasions but is weakened by their cost.
provenance: sources to check: Farris, Japan to 1600 (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Ming dynasty, 1368 to 1644
upsert.description: Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant rebel, founds the Ming; his successors move the capital to Beijing, build the Forbidden City and the brick Great Wall, send Zheng He's fleets, then turn inward; by the 1500s a commercial economy runs on silver from Japan and the Americas. Cold, drought, epidemics, fiscal crisis and rebellion bring it down in 1644.
provenance: sources to check: Brook, The Troubled Empire (2010)

upsert.boundary: The Mongol invasions of Japan, 1274 and 1281
upsert.description: Kublai Khan's fleets of Mongol, Chinese and Korean troops land in Kyushu twice; samurai and coastal walls hold them, and storms, later called kamikaze, the divine wind, wreck the fleets.
provenance: sources to check: Conlan, In Little Need of Divine Intervention (2001)

upsert.boundary: The Mughal empire, 1526 to 1857
upsert.description: Babur, a descendant of Timur and Genghis Khan, defeats the last Delhi sultan at Panipat (1526); Akbar (1556 to 1605) builds an empire of perhaps 100 million people with a salaried nobility and tolerance among faiths; Shah Jahan builds the Taj Mahal; Aurangzeb extends it furthest but leaves it at war, and after his death in 1707 it breaks into successor states, Maratha power and in the end British rule; the British depose the last emperor in 1857.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; population an estimate
sources to check: Richards, The Mughal Empire (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Afghanistan)

upsert.boundary: The Ottoman empire, about 1299 to 1922
upsert.description: From a frontier principality in north-west Anatolia, the Ottomans conquer the Balkans, take Constantinople (1453), Syria, Egypt and Arabia (1516 to 1517) and Iraq, and under Suleiman (1520 to 1566) besiege Vienna; their sultans claim the caliphate. Their story is not one long decline: they reform repeatedly, but lose the Balkans and North Africa in the 1800s, and the empire ends after defeat in the First World War.
provenance: sources to check: Finkel, Osman's Dream (2005)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia); Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Spain in the Philippines, 1565 to 1700
upsert.description: Legazpi founds the first Spanish settlement at Cebu (1565) and Manila (1571), the Asian end of the galleon trade; Spanish friars convert most lowland Filipinos from their local religions to Catholicism within a century, while the Muslim sultanates of Mindanao and Sulu resist.
provenance: sources to check: Phelan, The Hispanization of the Philippines (1959)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (the Philippines); Europe (Southern Europe: Spain)

upsert.boundary: The Portuguese in Asian waters, 1498 to 1641
upsert.description: Vasco da Gama reaches Calicut in May 1498 by sailing around Africa; the Portuguese then take Goa (1510), Malacca (1511) and Hormuz (1515), reach Japan (1543) and settle at Macau (1557), using armed ships to tax the Indian Ocean trade through passes rather than conquering inland; the Dutch take Malacca from them in 1641.
provenance: sources to check: Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia 1500–1700 (2nd ed. 2012)
upsert.region: Asia (Southern, South-eastern, Eastern and Western Asia); Europe (Southern Europe: Portugal)

upsert.boundary: The High Qing, 1683 to 1796
upsert.description: Having taken Taiwan (1683), the Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong emperors double the empire's area by conquering Mongolia, Xinjiang and Tibet; with peace and New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes, China's population grows from perhaps 150 million to about 300 million, a third of humanity, the largest share any state has held. The White Lotus rebellion (1796) marks the end of the high period.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; population figures are estimates
sources to check: Rowe, China's Last Empire (2009); Perdue, China Marches West (2005)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Mongolia, Taiwan), Central Asia (Xinjiang)

upsert.boundary: Safavid Iran, 1501 to 1736
upsert.description: Shah Ismail, head of a Sufi order, conquers Iran and imposes Twelver Shi'ism, making Iran the Shia land it remains; under Shah Abbas (1588 to 1629) Isfahan is rebuilt as a capital of mosques, gardens and bazaars; Afghan invaders end the dynasty's power in 1722, and it ends formally in 1736.
provenance: sources to check: Newman, Safavid Iran (2006)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (Iran, Afghanistan), Western Asia (Iraq, the Caucasus)

upsert.boundary: The Seljuk Turks, 1037 to 1194
upsert.description: Turkic nomads from Central Asia, converted to Sunni Islam, conquer Iran, enter Baghdad as the caliph's sultans (1055) and defeat Byzantium at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turkic settlement; their madrasas spread a standard Sunni learning.
provenance: sources to check: Peacock, The Great Seljuk Empire (2015)
upsert.region: Asia: Central Asia, Southern Asia (Iran), Western Asia (Iraq, Anatolia, Syria)

upsert.boundary: Guru Nanak and the Sikh Gurus, about 1499 to 1708
upsert.description: In the Punjab, Guru Nanak teaches devotion to one formless God beyond Hindu and Muslim ritual and caste; nine Gurus follow him, compile the Adi Granth (1604) and resist Mughal persecution, and Guru Gobind Singh founds the Khalsa (1699) before naming the scripture itself the last Guru.
provenance: sources to check: Grewal, The Sikhs of the Punjab (1990)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan: the Punjab)

upsert.boundary: Song China and its commercial revolution, 960 to 1279
upsert.description: The Song govern through officials chosen by examination, print books in great numbers, issue the first government paper money and grow early-ripening Champa rice; China's population passes 100 million, and Kaifeng and later Hangzhou hold a million people or more, the largest cities in the world. Iron and coal, the compass at sea and gunpowder weapons grow with them, and Zhu Xi's Neo-Confucianism becomes the orthodoxy of later dynasties. The north falls to the Jurchen in 1127 and the south to the Mongols in 1279.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; city populations are estimates
sources to check: Elvin, The Pattern of the Chinese Past (1973); Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule (2009)

upsert.boundary: Srivijaya, about 671 to 1377
upsert.description: From Palembang in Sumatra, a Malay maritime power controls the Straits of Malacca and Sunda and the trade between China and India; Chinese pilgrims stop there to learn Sanskrit and Buddhist texts. In Java, the Sailendra kings build Borobudur (about 800).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its power had faded long before 1377
sources to check: Wolters, Early Indonesian Commerce (1967); Miksic, Singapore and the Silk Road of the Sea (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Tang dynasty, 618 to 907
upsert.description: The Tang rule from Chang'an, a city of perhaps a million people and among the largest in the world, over an empire reaching into Central Asia; they recruit some officials by examination, codify law, patronize Buddhism until the persecution of 845, and host Sogdian, Persian and Arab merchants. The poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu marks its height. After the An Lushan rebellion regional governors hold real power, and the dynasty ends in 907.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Chang'an's population is an estimate
sources to check: Lewis, China's Cosmopolitan Empire (2009)

upsert.boundary: Timur's conquests, 1370 to 1405
upsert.description: From Samarkand, Timur conquers from Anatolia to Delhi, sacking Baghdad, Delhi and Damascus with mass killings, defeats the Ottomans at Ankara (1402) and dies marching on China; his successors make Samarkand and Herat centres of Persian art and astronomy.
provenance: sources to check: Manz, The Rise and Rule of Tamerlane (1989)
upsert.region: Asia: Central Asia, Southern Asia (Iran, Afghanistan, India), Western Asia

upsert.boundary: Tokugawa Japan, 1603 to 1868
upsert.description: The Tokugawa shoguns keep two and a half centuries of peace from Edo, make the lords spend alternate years at court, expel missionaries, persecute Christians and close the country to all but Dutch and Chinese traders at Nagasaki (1639); Edo grows to a million people, literacy spreads, and kabuki, ukiyo-e and haiku flourish.
provenance: sources to check: Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch East India Company, 1602 to 1799
upsert.description: The first joint-stock company with permanent shares, chartered with powers of war, takes Batavia (1619), kills or expels most of the Banda islanders to monopolize nutmeg (1621), takes Malacca and Ceylon from Portugal, and trades at Nagasaki as the only Europeans Japan admits; it is dissolved in debt in 1799.
provenance: sources to check: Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (2003)
upsert.region: Asia (South-eastern Asia: Indonesia; Southern Asia: Sri Lanka; Eastern Asia: Japan); Europe (Western Europe: the Netherlands)

upsert.boundary: Printing in East Asia: woodblocks and the first movable type, about 700 to 1050
upsert.description: Buddhist charms are printed from carved woodblocks in China and Korea by the 700s; the Diamond Sutra from Dunhuang (868) is the oldest dated printed book; the Song print the classics in great runs; about 1040 Bi Sheng makes movable type of baked clay. In Korea, metal movable type prints the Jikji in 1377.
provenance: sources to check: Tsien, Paper and Printing, in Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)

upsert.boundary: The Yuan dynasty, 1271 to 1368
upsert.description: Kublai Khan proclaims a Chinese-style dynasty, rules from Dadu (Beijing), completes the conquest of the Song (1279) and joins China to the Mongol world; merchants and envoys, Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta among them, travel its roads. Plague, floods and the Red Turban rebellions bring it down.
provenance: sources to check: Rossabi, Khubilai Khan (1988); Brook, The Troubled Empire (2010)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Mongolia, Korea as vassal)

upsert.boundary: Zheng He's voyages, 1405 to 1433
upsert.description: The Muslim eunuch admiral Zheng He leads seven fleets of up to 250 ships and some 27,000 men for the Yongle emperor to South-east Asia, India, Arabia and East Africa, collecting tribute and giraffes; after 1433 the court ends the voyages and later restricts private overseas trade.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; fleet sizes come from Ming sources and may be inflated
sources to check: Dreyer, Zheng He: China and the Oceans in the Early Ming Dynasty (2007)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern, South-eastern, Southern and Western Asia); Africa (Eastern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Ottomans take Constantinople, 6 April to 29 May 1453
upsert.description: After a siege of seven weeks in which great bronze cannon batter the land walls, Mehmed II takes the city and ends the Byzantine empire, the last remnant of Rome; as Istanbul it becomes the Ottoman capital.
provenance: sources to check: Runciman, The Fall of Constantinople 1453 (1965); Crowley, Constantinople: The Last Great Siege (2005)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Turkey); Europe (Southern Europe: the Byzantine state)

upsert.boundary: The Crusades in the Levant, 1096 to 1291
upsert.description: Answering a Byzantine appeal and the Pope's call, armies from Western Europe take Jerusalem (1099) and found Crusader states on the Levant coast; Saladin retakes Jerusalem (1187), the Fourth Crusade sacks Christian Constantinople (1204), and the Mamluks take Acre, the last Crusader city, in 1291.
provenance: sources to check: Riley-Smith, The Crusades: A History (3rd ed. 2014); Tyerman, God's War (2006)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: the Levant, Anatolia); Europe (Western and Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, in later crusades)

upsert.boundary: Silver joins the world in one trade, 1571 to 1644
upsert.description: From 1571 the Manila galleons carry silver from Mexico and Potosí across the Pacific, while Portuguese and Dutch ships carry Japanese and American silver to China, whose economy and taxes have turned to silver; for the first time every inhabited continent trades in one system. Silk, porcelain and tea go the other way.
provenance: sources to check: Flynn and Giráldez 1995, Journal of World History 6; von Glahn, Fountain of Fortune (1996)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern and South-eastern Asia); Americas (Latin America: Mexico, the Andes); Europe

upsert.boundary: Gunpowder, from China to the world, about 850 to 1350
upsert.description: Chinese alchemists searching for elixirs mix saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal by the 800s; the Song arm soldiers with fire lances and bombs; the first guns, metal barrels firing projectiles, appear in China by the late 1200s. The Mongol wars carry the knowledge west, and cannon are used in Europe and the Islamic world by the 1320s and 1340s.
provenance: sources to check: Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 7 (1986); Andrade, The Gunpowder Age (2016)
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern Asia: China; Western Asia); Europe

upsert.boundary: Muhammad, the Arab conquests and the Umayyad caliphate, 610 to 750
upsert.description: In Mecca and Medina Muhammad preaches submission to one God and unites the tribes of Arabia (610 to 632); within a century his successors conquer the Sasanian empire, Byzantine Syria and Egypt, North Africa and Spain, and reach the Indus and Central Asia. The Umayyad caliphs rule from Damascus one of the largest empires yet; conversion to Islam among the conquered, slow at first, follows over the next centuries. The Abbasid revolution ends Umayyad rule in 750.
provenance: sources to check: Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010); Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Arabia, the Levant, Iraq; Southern Asia: Iran; Central Asia); Africa (Northern Africa); Europe (Southern Europe: Iberia)

changes.value: Asia's own history from 600 to 1800, inside its eras. Caliphates, Tang and Song: the rise of Islam and the Arab conquests, the Tang and the An Lushan rebellion, the Abbasids and the translation movement, Srivijaya, Heian Japan, printing in East Asia, gunpowder, Angkor, the Cholas, the Song commercial revolution, the Seljuks and the Crusades. The Mongol era: the conquests, the sack of Baghdad, the Yuan, the invasions of Japan, the Black Death, Kamakura, the Delhi Sultanate, Timur, the Ming, the Ottomans and Joseon. Gunpowder empires and the oceanic trade: Zheng He, Hangul, the fall of Constantinople, the Portuguese and the Dutch companies, the Safavids, the Sikh Gurus, the Mughals, Islam in island South-east Asia, Spain in the Philippines, the silver trade, Japan's unification and the Imjin war, the Tokugawa, the Ming–Qing transition, the High Qing and the East India Company's conquest of Bengal. Five are world Events in humanity's eras: the rise of Islam, gunpowder, the Crusades, the fall of Constantinople and the silver trade. The Events that turn a world measure name it: the Muslim share (the rise of Islam, the Delhi Sultanate, Islam in the islands), the Christian and local shares (the Philippines), the largest city (Chang'an, Baghdad, Kaifeng and Hangzhou), the largest polity (the High Qing) and trade as a share of output (the silver trade). Existing world Events that belong to Asia's history (the Mongol conquests, the Black Death, the Ming–Qing transition) are placed in its eras and regions.

upsert.boundary: The Soviet war in Afghanistan, 1979 to 1989
upsert.description: Soviet troops invade (December 1979) to save a communist government; Islamist mujahideen armed by the United States, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia fight them for nine years; about a million Afghans die and five million flee before the Soviets withdraw (February 1989), and civil war and the Taliban follow.
provenance: sources to check: Braithwaite, Afghantsy (2011); Coll, Ghost Wars (2004)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (Afghanistan, Pakistan); Europe (Eastern Europe: the Soviet Union)

upsert.boundary: The Armenian genocide, 1915 to 1917
upsert.description: The Ottoman government deports the Armenians of Anatolia toward the Syrian desert; through massacre, death marches and starvation perhaps a million or more die, and Assyrian and Greek Christians are also killed in great numbers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; totals range from about 600,000 to 1.5 million
sources to check: Suny, 'They Can Live in the Desert but Nowhere Else' (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Asian financial crisis, 1997 to 1998
upsert.description: Starting with the fall of the Thai baht (July 1997), foreign capital flees Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea and Malaysia; currencies and output collapse, Indonesia's economy shrinks by about 13% in 1998 and Suharto falls, and the IMF imposes austere rescue terms.
provenance: sources to check: Radelet and Sachs 1998, Brookings Papers on Economic Activity
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia), Eastern Asia (South Korea)

upsert.boundary: Bangladesh's war of independence, 1971
upsert.description: When Pakistan's army cracks down on East Bengal after the Awami League wins the 1970 election, hundreds of thousands to perhaps three million people are killed and ten million flee to India; India intervenes in December and Bangladesh becomes independent.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is fiercely disputed
sources to check: Raghavan, 1971 (2013); Bass, The Blood Telegram (2013)

upsert.boundary: The Bengal famine, 1943 to 1944
upsert.description: After a cyclone, crop disease and the loss of Burmese rice imports to Japan's conquest, wartime inflation, hoarding and the colonial government's refusal to stop exports or call a famine kill about three million people in Bengal.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the weight of each cause is debated
sources to check: Sen, Poverty and Famines (1981); Ó Gráda, Eating People Is Wrong (2015)

upsert.boundary: The British Raj, 1858 to 1947
upsert.description: The Crown rules India through a viceroy, a small civil service and princely allies; railways, canals and telegraphs are built, and English education creates a new middle class, while India's income per head barely grows, famines kill tens of millions and India's taxes and trade surplus help pay for Britain's empire.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the Raj's economic effect is debated
sources to check: Roy, The Economic History of India 1857–2010 (4th ed. 2020); Tomlinson, The Economy of Modern India (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: Southern Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Burma until 1937); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: China joins the WTO and becomes the world's workshop, from 2001
upsert.description: China enters the World Trade Organization (December 2001); its exports grow fivefold in a decade, it becomes the largest manufacturer (2010) and trader in goods (2013), lifts hundreds of millions out of poverty, and displaces manufacturing jobs in rich countries, the 'China shock'.
provenance: sources to check: Autor, Dorn and Hanson 2016, Annual Review of Economics 8; Naughton, The Chinese Economy (2nd ed. 2018)

upsert.boundary: China's civil war, 1927 to 1949
upsert.description: Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalists turn on their Communist allies (1927); the Communists survive the Long March (1934 to 1935) and grow during the war with Japan, then defeat the Nationalists in 1946 to 1949; Mao proclaims the People's Republic in October 1949 and the Nationalists withdraw to Taiwan.
provenance: sources to check: Westad, Decisive Encounters (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Cultural Revolution, 1966 to 1976
upsert.description: Mao mobilizes students as Red Guards against party officials, teachers and 'old' culture; schools and universities close, millions are persecuted and sent to the countryside, and perhaps one to two million die, before the arrest of the Gang of Four ends it in October 1976.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: MacFarquhar and Schoenhals, Mao's Last Revolution (2006)

upsert.boundary: The El Niño famines in India and China, 1876 to 1902
upsert.description: Monsoon failures in strong El Niño years bring famine to India (1876 to 1878, 1896 to 1897, 1899 to 1900) and north China (1876 to 1879), and also to Brazil and Ethiopia; perhaps 30 to 50 million people die. Grain exports, relief that demanded hard labour for meagre rations, and weakened Qing granaries made drought into mass death.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; death tolls are very uncertain
sources to check: Davis, Late Victorian Holocausts (2001); Edgerton-Tarpley, Tears from Iron (2008)

upsert.boundary: East and South Asia's fall in births, 1970 to 2025
upsert.description: With falling child deaths, schooling, cities, family-planning programmes and, in China, the one-child policy (1980 to 2015), births per woman fall from five or six to below replacement across East Asia, Iran, Thailand and most of India's states; South Korea's reaches 0.72 in 2023, the lowest ever recorded for a country, and Japan's, China's and Korea's populations begin to shrink.
provenance: sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024; Statistics Korea
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia, Southern Asia, South-eastern Asia

upsert.boundary: The Tōhoku earthquake, tsunami and Fukushima disaster, March 2011
upsert.description: A magnitude 9.0 earthquake off north-east Japan raises a tsunami that kills about 18,000 people and causes meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant, forcing more than 150,000 people from their homes and turning several countries away from nuclear power.
provenance: sources to check: Japan National Police Agency figures; IAEA, The Fukushima Daiichi Accident (2015)

upsert.boundary: The Hamas attack of 7 October 2023 and the war in Gaza
upsert.description: Hamas fighters kill about 1,200 people in Israel and take some 250 hostages; Israel's war in Gaza kills tens of thousands of Palestinians, displaces most of Gaza's 2.1 million people and leaves the territory in ruins, and spreads to Lebanon, Yemen and Iran before a ceasefire in October 2025.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are contested and still being counted
sources to check: UN OCHA reports; Gaza Ministry of Health and independent assessments
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Israel and Palestine, Lebanon, Yemen, Iran)

upsert.boundary: Oil in the Gulf, from 1938
upsert.description: After oil is found in Bahrain (1932), Saudi Arabia (1938) and Kuwait, the Gulf becomes the world's main source of oil; nationalizations and OPEC (1960) shift control to the producing states, and oil revenue turns small desert monarchies into some of the richest states per head on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the Gulf states, Iraq), Southern Asia (Iran)

upsert.boundary: Iraq invades Kuwait and the Gulf War, 1990 to 1991
upsert.description: Iraq occupies Kuwait (August 1990); a coalition of 35 states led by the United States expels it in a six-week air and ground war (January to February 1991), and sanctions on Iraq follow for twelve years.
provenance: sources to check: Freedman and Karsh, The Gulf Conflict 1990–1991 (1993)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia)

upsert.boundary: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, 6 and 9 August 1945
upsert.description: American bombers drop atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki, killing about 110,000 to 210,000 people by the end of 1945; with the Soviet declaration of war, they bring Japan's surrender. They remain the only nuclear weapons used in war.
provenance: sources to check: Hasegawa, Racing the Enemy (2005); Rhodes, The Making of the Atomic Bomb (1986)

upsert.boundary: India overtakes China as the most populous country, 2023
upsert.description: By the UN's estimate India's population passes China's, at about 1.43 billion each, around April 2023; China has been the most populous state for most of recorded history.
provenance: sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2022 and 2024

upsert.boundary: India's independence movement, 1885 to 1947
upsert.description: From the founding of the Indian National Congress (1885), nationalists press for self-rule; after 1915 Gandhi turns the movement into mass non-violent campaigns of non-cooperation (1920 to 1922), the Salt March (1930) and Quit India (1942), while the Muslim League comes to demand a separate Pakistan.
provenance: sources to check: Brown, Modern India (2nd ed. 1994); Guha, Gandhi: The Years That Changed the World (2018)

upsert.boundary: The Indian rebellion, 1857 to 1858
upsert.description: Sepoys of the Bengal army mutiny at Meerut (May 1857) and proclaim the old Mughal emperor their ruler; the revolt spreads across north India and is crushed with great brutality. The British exile the last emperor and the Crown takes India from the East India Company.
provenance: sources to check: Wagner, The Great Fear of 1857 (2010); Dalrymple, The Last Mughal (2006)

upsert.boundary: Indonesia's revolution, 1945 to 1949
upsert.description: Sukarno and Hatta proclaim independence two days after Japan's surrender; the Dutch fight four years to retake their colony before American pressure makes them transfer sovereignty (December 1949).
provenance: sources to check: Ricklefs, A History of Modern Indonesia since c. 1200 (4th ed. 2008)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia); Europe (Western Europe: the Netherlands)

upsert.boundary: The Iran–Iraq War, 1980 to 1988
upsert.description: Saddam Hussein invades revolutionary Iran (September 1980); after eight years of trench warfare, human-wave attacks and poison gas, perhaps half a million or more dead, the war ends in a ceasefire with the border unchanged.
provenance: sources to check: Murray and Woods, The Iran–Iraq War (2014)

upsert.boundary: Iran's revolution, 1978 to 1979
upsert.description: Mass protests against the Shah's autocracy bring down the monarchy; Ayatollah Khomeini returns from exile (February 1979) and founds an Islamic Republic ruled by a Shia jurist, which takes American diplomats hostage and sets out to export its revolution.
provenance: sources to check: Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Iraq war, 2003 to 2011
upsert.description: An American-led invasion overthrows Saddam Hussein (March to April 2003); disbanding the army and the Baath party feeds an insurgency and a sectarian civil war in which a few hundred thousand Iraqis die, before American troops leave at the end of 2011.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; death tolls range widely
sources to check: Iraq Body Count; Gordon and Trainor, The Endgame (2012)

upsert.boundary: Israel's founding and the war of 1948
upsert.description: After the UN votes to partition Palestine (November 1947), civil war breaks out; Israel declares independence (May 1948) and defeats the armies of its Arab neighbours; about 700,000 Palestinians flee or are expelled, the Nakba, and hundreds of thousands of Jews later leave or are driven from Arab countries.

upsert.boundary: The Arab–Israeli conflict, from 1947
upsert.description: From the UN partition plan (1947) and Israel's founding, through wars in 1948, 1956, 1967, 1973 and 1982, the occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, the intifadas, the Oslo accords and the Gaza wars, Israelis and Palestinians fight over the same land, drawing in the Arab states and the great powers.
provenance: sources to check: Morris, Righteous Victims (1999); Khalidi, The Hundred Years' War on Palestine (2020)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Israel and Palestine, Egypt's Sinai, Jordan, Syria, Lebanon)

upsert.boundary: Japan's war in China and the Pacific, 1931 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan seizes Manchuria (1931), invades China proper (1937), massacring civilians at Nanjing, and in 1941 attacks Pearl Harbor and conquers South-east Asia; perhaps 15 to 20 million Chinese and millions more across Asia die. Defeat at sea, the firebombing of its cities, the atomic bombs and the Soviet attack end the war in August 1945.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; Chinese deaths are very uncertain
sources to check: Mitter, China's War with Japan 1937–1945 (2013); Spector, Eagle Against the Sun (1985)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Japan, Korea), South-eastern Asia; Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia); Americas (Northern America: Hawaii)

upsert.boundary: Japan rules Korea, 1910 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan annexes Korea (August 1910) and rules it as a colony: land surveys, railways and later factories, the suppression of the March First movement (1919), forced name changes and the Korean language banned from schools, and in the war mass labour conscription and the sexual slavery of 'comfort women'.
provenance: sources to check: Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

upsert.boundary: Japan's economic miracle, 1950 to 1973
upsert.description: Rebuilt from defeat, Japan's economy grows by nearly 10% a year, from steel and ships to cars and electronics, on high saving, guided industrial policy and open American markets; by 1968 it is the second-largest economy outside the communist world.
provenance: sources to check: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle (1982)

upsert.boundary: The Khmer Rouge in Cambodia, 1975 to 1979
upsert.description: Pol Pot's Khmer Rouge empty the cities, abolish money and religion and force the population into labour camps; by execution, starvation and disease about 1.5 to 2 million people, a fifth or more of Cambodians, die before Vietnam invades and ends the regime.
provenance: sources to check: Kiernan, The Pol Pot Regime (3rd ed. 2008)

upsert.boundary: The Korean War, 1950 to 1953
upsert.description: North Korea invades the South (June 1950); a US-led UN force pushes north to the Chinese border, China's armies drive it back, and the war ends in an armistice near the 38th parallel (July 1953) after perhaps three million deaths, leaving Korea divided.
provenance: sources to check: Cumings, The Korean War (2010)

upsert.boundary: Meiji Japan, 1868 to 1912
upsert.description: Young samurai overthrow the shogunate in the emperor's name (1868), abolish the domains and the samurai class, send missions to learn from the West, build railways, factories, a conscript army and compulsory schools, and adopt a constitution (1889); within forty years Japan is an industrial and imperial power.
provenance: sources to check: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan (2000)

upsert.boundary: The Opium Wars, 1839 to 1860
upsert.description: When the Qing destroy British opium at Canton (1839), Britain goes to war and by the Treaty of Nanjing (1842) takes Hong Kong and opens five ports; in the second war (1856 to 1860) Britain and France occupy Beijing and burn the Summer Palace. The unequal treaties open China to foreign trade, missionaries and extraterritorial law.
provenance: sources to check: Lovell, The Opium War (2011)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China); Europe (Northern and Western Europe: Britain, France)

upsert.boundary: The Ottoman empire is partitioned, 1916 to 1923
upsert.description: Britain and France plan the division of the Arab lands (Sykes–Picot, 1916), Britain promises a Jewish national home in Palestine (1917), and after the Ottoman defeat they rule Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Palestine and Transjordan as League of Nations mandates; in Anatolia, Mustafa Kemal's nationalists defeat the Greek invasion and found the Republic of Turkey (October 1923).
provenance: sources to check: Rogan, The Fall of the Ottomans (2015); Fromkin, A Peace to End All Peace (1989)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Turkey, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Israel and Palestine, Jordan); Europe (Western and Northern Europe: France, Britain)

upsert.boundary: Independence and the partition of India, 1947
upsert.description: Britain hands power to two states, India and Pakistan (East and West), at midnight on 14 to 15 August 1947; as the borders cut through Punjab and Bengal, about 15 million people flee across them and perhaps 200,000 to two million are killed in communal violence.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is very uncertain
sources to check: Khan, The Great Partition (2007)

upsert.boundary: Perry's Black Ships open Japan, 1853 to 1854
upsert.description: An American squadron under Commodore Perry sails into Edo Bay (July 1853) and returns with more ships to force the Treaty of Kanagawa (March 1854), ending two centuries of seclusion; unequal treaties with the Western powers follow.
provenance: sources to check: Jansen, The Making of Modern Japan (2000)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (Japan); Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: Mao's People's Republic, 1949 to 1976
upsert.description: The Communist Party unifies China, carries out a land reform in which perhaps a million or more landlords are killed, collectivizes farming, launches the Great Leap Forward and its famine and then the Cultural Revolution; it also roughly doubles life expectancy and spreads basic schooling. Religion is suppressed and the state teaches atheism.
provenance: sources to check: Dikötter, The Tragedy of Liberation (2013); MacFarquhar (ed.), The Politics of China (3rd ed. 2011)

upsert.boundary: The Russo-Japanese War, 1904 to 1905
upsert.description: Japan attacks Russia's fleet at Port Arthur, wins the siege and the battle of Mukden, and destroys Russia's Baltic fleet at Tsushima; the first defeat of a European great power by an Asian one in modern war, it inspires nationalists from Egypt to India and helps provoke Russia's 1905 revolution.
provenance: sources to check: Paine, The Japanese Empire (2017)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (Manchuria, Korea, Japan); Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia)

upsert.boundary: Asia's share of humanity eases from 61% to 58.5%, 2000 to 2025
upsert.description: Births fall below replacement across East Asia, in Iran, Thailand and much of India, while Africa's population keeps growing fast: Asia's share of humanity eases from 61% to 58.5%, the first fall since 1930. China's population peaks in 2021.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares (2000 60.8%, 2025 58.54%)
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024

upsert.boundary: Asia's share of humanity falls from 66% to 55%, 1800 to 1930
upsert.description: Asia's people grow from about 650 million to 1.13 billion, but the world's grow faster, from about 1 to 2.07 billion, as Europe's and the Americas' populations multiply: Asia's share falls from 66% to 55%. Its own catastrophes add to the fall: the Taiping and other wars of the 1850s to 1870s, the El Niño famines of 1876 to 1902, plague in India from 1896 and the 1918 influenza, which kill well over a hundred million people between them.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares (1800 65.9%, 1930 54.85%)
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects and its historical estimates; McEvedy and Jones, Atlas of World Population History (1978); Maddison Project

upsert.boundary: Asia's share of humanity recovers from 55% to 61%, 1930 to 2000
upsert.description: Vaccines, antibiotics, DDT against malaria, clean water and the green revolution cut deaths across Asia from the 1940s, while births stay high until the 1970s: China's people grow from about 500 million to 1.27 billion and South Asia's from about 400 million to 1.4 billion. Europe's births fall at the same time, and Asia's share rises back to 61% despite the war with Japan and China's great famine.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares (1930 54.85%, 2000 60.8%)
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024

upsert.boundary: The First Sino-Japanese War, 1894 to 1895
upsert.description: Japan's modern army and navy defeat China over Korea; by the Treaty of Shimonoseki China gives up Taiwan, recognizes Korea's independence from it and pays a large indemnity, revealing how far the Qing's own reforms lagged behind Japan's.
provenance: sources to check: Paine, The Sino-Japanese War of 1894–1895 (2003)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (China, Korea, Japan, Taiwan)

upsert.boundary: The Six-Day War, June 1967
upsert.description: Israel defeats Egypt, Jordan and Syria and takes Sinai, Gaza, the West Bank, East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, beginning an occupation that shapes the conflict ever since.
provenance: sources to check: Oren, Six Days of War (2002)
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Israel and Palestine, Jordan, Syria); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt)

upsert.boundary: The Syrian civil war, 2011 to 2024
upsert.description: The Assad regime meets peaceful protests (March 2011) with force; civil war, Russian and Iranian intervention, chemical attacks and the Islamic State's rise kill about half a million people and drive 13 million from their homes, many to Turkey and Europe; rebels take Damascus and Assad flees in December 2024.
provenance: sources to check: UNHCR; Syrian Observatory for Human Rights
upsert.region: Asia: Western Asia (Syria, Iraq, Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan); Europe (as refuge)

upsert.boundary: The Tiananmen protests and massacre, April to June 1989
upsert.description: Students and workers occupy Tiananmen Square and protest in many cities for political reform and against corruption; on 3 and 4 June the army clears Beijing, killing hundreds to perhaps thousands, and the party chooses economic reform without political liberalization.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the death toll is unknown
sources to check: Lim, The People's Republic of Amnesia (2014)

upsert.boundary: The Asian tigers, 1962 to 1997
upsert.description: South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong and Singapore grow from poverty to rich-country incomes in a generation, through land reform, schooling, high saving and exports of manufactures; South Korea's income per head rises about tenfold. Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia follow from the 1970s.
provenance: sources to check: World Bank, The East Asian Miracle (1993); Studwell, How Asia Works (2013)
upsert.region: Asia: Eastern Asia (South Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong), South-eastern Asia (Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia)

upsert.boundary: The Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami, 26 December 2004
upsert.description: A magnitude 9.1 earthquake off Sumatra sends waves across the Indian Ocean, killing about 230,000 people in Indonesia, Sri Lanka, India, Thailand and as far as Somalia, the deadliest tsunami recorded.
provenance: sources to check: Lay et al. 2005, Science 308
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Indonesia, Thailand), Southern Asia (Sri Lanka, India); Africa (Eastern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Indochina wars, 1946 to 1975
upsert.description: The Viet Minh fight France until Dien Bien Phu (1954) and the division of Vietnam; the Communist North then fights to unify the country against the South and, from 1965, half a million American troops; the war spreads to Laos and Cambodia, and ends with the fall of Saigon (April 1975), after two to three million deaths.
provenance: sources to check: Logevall, Embers of War (2012); Herring, America's Longest War (5th ed. 2013)
upsert.region: Asia: South-eastern Asia (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia); Americas (Northern America: the United States); Europe (Western Europe: France)

upsert.boundary: The 1911 revolution ends imperial China, 1911 to 1912
upsert.description: A mutiny at Wuchang (October 1911) spreads to most provinces; the last Qing emperor abdicates (February 1912) and a republic is proclaimed, ending more than two thousand years of imperial rule, but power soon passes to Yuan Shikai and then to warlords.
provenance: sources to check: Spence, The Search for Modern China (3rd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: The oil shocks, 1973 to 1980
upsert.description: In the October 1973 war, Arab producers embargo the United States and the Netherlands and the price of oil quadruples; after Iran's revolution (1979) it more than doubles again. provenance: sources to check: Yergin, The Prize (1991)

upsert.boundary: The 11 September attacks, 2001

upsert.boundary: The war on terror, 2001 to 2021

changes.value: Asia's own history from 1800 to 2025, in its two last eras. Western dominance, reform and revolution: Asia's share of humanity falls from 66% to 55% (1800 to 1930), the Opium Wars, the Taiping war, Perry's ships, the Indian rebellion and the Raj, Meiji Japan, the El Niño famines, the wars of 1894 and 1904, Japan's annexation of Korea, the 1911 revolution, the Armenian genocide, the partition of the Ottoman empire, India's independence movement, China's civil war, Japan's war in China and the Pacific, the Bengal famine and Hiroshima. Independence and Asia's rise: Asia's share recovers to 61% (1930 to 2000) and eases to 58.5% (2000 to 2025), partition, Indonesia's revolution, the Arab–Israeli conflict, Mao's China and the Cultural Revolution, the Korean and Vietnam wars, Japan's miracle and the Asian tigers, Gulf oil and the oil shocks, Bangladesh, the Khmer Rouge, Iran's revolution, the Soviet war in Afghanistan, the Iran–Iraq and Gulf wars, Tiananmen, the Asian financial crisis, China's entry into the world economy, 11 September and the war on terror, the Iraq and Syrian wars, the 2004 tsunami, Fukushima, East Asia's fall in births and India becoming the most populous country. Existing Events of Asia's history (the Taiping war, the Great Leap and the famine, China's reform, India's democracy and liberalization, the green revolution, the 1918 drought and influenza, COVID-19) are placed in its eras and regions. The share Events name Asia's measure, Mao's China the share with no religion, and India's overtaking of China the largest polity.

changes.value: 6948396084e70e5ffdd0e6fff79fd39b33032d5de0d7a231aabceae61d240e4d

Weighing the causes of the turns in the regional shares and of the turning points left unweighed by earlier passes. A share of humanity falls either because the region's own people die or are not born, or because others grow faster, so every share question is set against the contrast of the region growing at the world's rate (ContrastClass#7398) and the base rate of growth elsewhere is read as a cause in its own right (BaseRateInclude#1e63). A fall is measured as the percentage points lost, so that a cause makes it larger; a rise as the share reached. Each reading without a cause recomputes the share from rough population totals: the people lost, with the children they would have had by the end date, added back to the region and to the world. Europe's own growth, which also lowers Asia's and Africa's shares in the 1800s, is not yet an Event; the Europe pass adds it.

upsert.description: Carthage's last wars, ending in its destruction.
Greek writing returns with the alphabet, and with it written laws and Homer's epics.
The plague kills perhaps a tenth of the empire's people and strains its army and taxes.
Persia invades Greece after the Ionian Greeks, its subjects, revolt with Athenian help.
An Event of the era, in Asia's own history.
