upsert.boundary: The alphabet: Phoenician letters and the Greek vowels, about 1050 to 750 BCE
upsert.description: Phoenician scribes write with 22 letters for consonants alone; the Greeks borrow them about 800 BCE and add vowels, the first full alphabet, from which Latin, Cyrillic and most of the world's alphabets descend. The Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic scripts grow from the same Phoenician root.
provenance: sources to check: Powell, Writing: Theory and History of the Technology of Civilization (2009)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Phoenicia); Europe (Southern Europe: Greece)

upsert.boundary: Jesus and the rise of Christianity, about 30 to 380
upsert.description: Jesus of Nazareth is crucified in Jerusalem about 30 CE; his followers, Paul above all, spread the faith through the cities of the Roman empire; despite persecutions it grows to perhaps a tenth of the empire's people by 300; Constantine converts (312) and Theodosius makes it the state religion (380).
provenance: inferred: as recalled; growth figures follow Stark's estimates, which are debated
sources to check: Stark, The Rise of Christianity (1996); MacCulloch, A History of Christianity (2009)
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Judea, Syria, Anatolia); Europe (Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, Carthage)

upsert.boundary: Al-Andalus: Muslim Iberia, 711 to 1492
upsert.description: Arab and Berber armies conquer most of Iberia (711 to 718); the Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (929 to 1031) is one of Europe's richest and most learned states, where Muslim, Jewish and Christian scholars work side by side; the Christian kingdoms push south, and Granada, the last Muslim state, falls in January 1492, the year Spain expels its Jews.
provenance: sources to check: Kennedy, Muslim Spain and Portugal (1996); Fierro, al-Andalus

upsert.boundary: Athenian democracy and the classical age, 508 to 322 BCE
upsert.description: Cleisthenes' reforms give power to the assembly of citizens; Athens leads the Greeks against Persia, builds the Parthenon and stages the tragedies of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, until Macedon ends its democracy in 322 BCE. Women, slaves and foreigners have no vote.
provenance: sources to check: Ober, The Rise and Fall of Classical Greece (2015)

upsert.boundary: Europe's first art: ivory figures, flutes and Chauvet, about 40,000 to 30,000 years ago
upsert.description: In the Swabian Jura people carve the Lion Man and the Venus of Hohle Fels from mammoth ivory and play flutes of bird bone (about 40,000 years ago); in Chauvet cave they paint lions, horses and rhinoceroses (about 36,000 years ago).
provenance: sources to check: Conard 2009, Nature 459; Quiles et al. 2016, PNAS 113

upsert.boundary: The Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire, 330 to 1453
upsert.description: From Constantine's new capital, the eastern half of the Roman empire outlives the west by a thousand years: Greek-speaking and Orthodox, it holds Europe's south-eastern flank against Persians, Arabs and Turks and converts the Slavs, until the Ottomans take Constantinople.
provenance: sources to check: Herrin, Byzantium (2007); Kaldellis, The New Roman Empire (2023)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans); Asia (Western Asia: Anatolia, Syria); Africa (Northern Africa: Egypt, until 641)

upsert.boundary: The Campanian Ignimbrite eruption, about 39,000 years ago
upsert.description: The largest eruption in Europe for 200,000 years, from the Phlegraean Fields near Naples, spreads ash from the Mediterranean to Russia and cools the climate for years; it may have hastened the end of the last Neanderthals and of early modern groups in the east.
provenance: exploring: its effect on people is debated
sources to check: Fedele et al. 2008, Journal of Human Evolution 55; Giaccio et al. 2017, Scientific Reports 7

upsert.boundary: Northern and eastern Europe become Christian, about 960 to 1100
upsert.description: Denmark's Harald Bluetooth (about 965), Poland's Mieszko (966), Kyiv's Vladimir (988), Hungary's Stephen (1000) and Iceland by vote of its assembly (1000) adopt Christianity, Latin or Orthodox, and the old gods fade; the Baltic peoples follow only in the 1200s and 1300s.
provenance: sources to check: Berend (ed.), Christianization and the Rise of Christian Monarchy (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Roman crisis of the third century, 235 to 284
upsert.description: Some twenty emperors in fifty years, most murdered; Persians, Goths and Alamanni break the frontiers, the Plague of Cyprian strikes, the silver coinage collapses, and the empire splits for a time into three, until Diocletian restores it with a larger army and heavier taxes.
provenance: sources to check: Harper, The Fate of Rome (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Western Europe); Asia (Western Asia); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: The Cucuteni–Trypillia mega-sites, about 4800 to 3000 BCE
upsert.description: Farmers between the Carpathians and the Dnieper build the largest settlements of their time, such as Talianki, with perhaps 10,000 people or more around 4000 BCE, and every few generations burn their own houses.
provenance: sources to check: Müller, Rassmann and Videiko (eds.), Trypillia Mega-Sites and European Prehistory (2016)

upsert.boundary: Doggerland drowns and Britain becomes an island, about 8000 to 6000 BCE
upsert.description: Rising seas flood the plain between Britain and the continent; around 6150 BCE the Storegga submarine slide off Norway sends a tsunami across the North Sea, and by about 6000 BCE Britain is cut off.
provenance: sources to check: Gaffney, Fitch and Smith, Europe's Lost World (2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Northern and Western Europe: the North Sea)

upsert.boundary: The Last Interglacial in Europe, about 130,000 to 115,000 years ago
upsert.description: For some fifteen thousand years Europe is warmer than today: hippopotamuses and straight-tusked elephants live along the Thames and the Rhine, forests reach Scandinavia and the sea stands several metres higher. Neanderthals live through it, mostly in the south.
provenance: sources to check: Turner, The Eemian interglacial (2000); Stringer, Homo Britannicus (2006)

upsert.boundary: Farmers from Anatolia spread across Europe, about 6700 to 4000 BCE
upsert.description: Farming families descended from Anatolia's first farmers reach Greece about 6700 BCE, the Danube and central Europe with the Linear Pottery culture about 5500 BCE, and Britain and Scandinavia about 4000 BCE, mostly replacing the hunter-gatherers and mixing with some of them: a wave of advance of about a kilometre a year (WaveOfAdvance#4cec).
provenance: sources to check: Ammerman and Cavalli-Sforza, The Neolithic Transition and the Genetics of Populations in Europe (1984); Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522

upsert.boundary: The Frankish kingdoms, from Clovis to the Treaty of Verdun, 481 to 843
upsert.description: Clovis unites the Franks and becomes a Catholic Christian; the Carolingians take over, Charles Martel stops an Umayyad army near Tours (732), and Charlemagne conquers from the Pyrenees to the Elbe and is crowned emperor in Rome (800); his grandsons divide the empire at Verdun into what become France and Germany.
provenance: sources to check: Wickham, The Inheritance of Rome (2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Western Europe: France, Germany, the Low Countries; Southern Europe: Italy)

upsert.boundary: Gravettian Europe, about 33,000 to 26,000 years ago
upsert.description: Mammoth hunters from France to Russia carve Venus figurines such as Willendorf's, fire clay figures at Dolní Věstonice, and bury some of their dead with thousands of ivory beads, as at Sunghir.
provenance: sources to check: Svoboda et al., in Gravettian studies; Trinkaus et al., The People of Sunghir (2014)

upsert.boundary: Greek philosophy and science, from Thales to Aristotle, about 600 to 322 BCE
upsert.description: From Miletus to Athens, thinkers seek natural causes and argue by reason: Thales, Pythagoras, Heraclitus, the atomists, Hippocratic medicine, Socrates, Plato's Academy and Aristotle's Lyceum.
provenance: sources to check: Lloyd, Early Greek Science (1970); Kenny, A New History of Western Philosophy vol. 1 (2004)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Greece, southern Italy); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia)

upsert.boundary: Archaic Greece: the city-states and their colonies, about 800 to 500 BCE
upsert.description: Greek-speaking communities organize as self-governing poleis, found colonies from Marseille to the Black Sea, hold the first Olympic games (776 BCE by tradition) and set down the Iliad and the Odyssey.
provenance: sources to check: Osborne, Greece in the Making (2nd ed. 2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia); Africa (Northern Africa: Cyrene)

upsert.boundary: Justinian's reconquest and law, 527 to 565
upsert.description: Justinian's generals retake North Africa from the Vandals and Italy from the Goths in long, ruinous wars; he codifies Roman law in the Corpus Juris Civilis, the root of most of Europe's later civil law, and builds Hagia Sophia; plague strikes in 541.
provenance: sources to check: Maas (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Age of Justinian (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Europe at the Last Glacial Maximum, about 26,000 to 19,000 years ago
upsert.description: Ice sheets cover Scandinavia, Britain and the Alps, and tundra and steppe the north; people withdraw to refuges in Iberia, southern France, Italy, the Balkans and Ukraine, where Solutrean flint-workers make thin laurel-leaf points.
provenance: sources to check: Posth et al. 2023, Nature 615

upsert.boundary: The Magdalenians: Lascaux and Altamira, about 20,000 to 14,000 years ago
upsert.description: As the ice retreats, Magdalenian hunters of reindeer and horse spread back over western and central Europe, paint the caves of Lascaux and Altamira, and carve spear-throwers and harpoons of antler.
provenance: sources to check: Bahn, Cave Art (2007)

upsert.boundary: Lords, serfs and the manor, about 800 to 1350
upsert.description: Across western Europe most peasants hold land from a lord in return for labour, rents and dues, tied to the manor as serfs, while a warrior aristocracy holds land for military service; serfdom fades in the west after the Black Death but deepens in the east.
provenance: sources to check: Bloch, Feudal Society (1939); Wickham, Medieval Europe (2016)

upsert.boundary: Megaliths: Carnac, Newgrange and Stonehenge, about 4500 to 2000 BCE
upsert.description: From Iberia and Brittany to Ireland and Scandinavia, farmers raise stone tombs, rows and circles; Newgrange's passage is lit by the midwinter sunrise (about 3200 BCE), and Stonehenge's great stones are raised about 2500 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Parker Pearson, Stonehenge (2012); Paulsson 2019, PNAS 116

upsert.boundary: Mesolithic foragers of Europe, about 9700 to 5500 BCE
upsert.description: In the forests of the Holocene, hunter-gatherers with dark skin and often blue eyes, as their genomes show, fish, gather hazelnuts and hunt deer and boar; some live in settled villages, such as Lepenski Vir on the Danube, until farmers arrive.
provenance: sources to check: Olalde et al. 2014, Nature 507 (La Braña); Brace et al. 2019, Nature Ecology & Evolution 3 (Cheddar Man)

upsert.boundary: The migration period, 376 to 568
upsert.description: Goths cross the Danube fleeing the Huns (376) and destroy a Roman army at Adrianople (378); Visigoths sack Rome (410), Vandals take Roman Africa (439), Attila's Huns raid Gaul and Italy, Franks, Angles and Saxons settle the west, and the Lombards enter Italy (568).
provenance: sources to check: Halsall, Barbarian Migrations and the Roman West (2007); Heather, Empires and Barbarians (2009)

upsert.boundary: Minoan Crete, about 2000 to 1450 BCE
upsert.description: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, painted with frescoes of bull-leaping, store and redistribute goods recorded in Linear A, still undeciphered; Mycenaean Greeks take over Knossos around 1450 BCE.
provenance: sources to check: Shelmerdine (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Aegean Bronze Age (2008)

upsert.boundary: Mycenaean Greece, about 1600 to 1180 BCE
upsert.description: Warrior kings rule from fortified palaces at Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes, write Greek in Linear B and trade across the Mediterranean, until their palaces are destroyed in the Bronze Age collapse; Homer's Trojan War remembers this world.
provenance: sources to check: Shelmerdine (ed.), The Cambridge Companion to the Aegean Bronze Age (2008)

upsert.boundary: The Neanderthals disappear, about 41,000 to 39,000 years ago
upsert.description: Within a few thousand years of Homo sapiens' arrival the last Neanderthals vanish across Europe. Competition, small and scattered populations, climate swings and absorption by interbreeding are all argued over; about 2% of the genome of people outside Africa is Neanderthal.
provenance: sources to check: Higham et al. 2014, Nature 512; Green et al. 2010, Science 328

upsert.boundary: Signs of Neanderthal minds, about 176,000 to 65,000 years ago
upsert.description: Neanderthals build rings of broken stalagmites deep in Bruniquel Cave (about 176,000 years ago), wear eagle talons as ornaments at Krapina (about 130,000), care for injured and disabled companions such as the old man of Shanidar, bury some of their dead, and may have painted red marks in Spanish caves more than 64,000 years ago.
provenance: exploring: the Spanish cave dates are disputed
sources to check: Jaubert et al. 2016, Nature 534; Radovčić et al. 2015, PLoS ONE 10; Hoffmann et al. 2018, Science 359
upsert.region: Europe (Western and Southern Europe); Asia (Western Asia: Shanidar)

upsert.boundary: The Peloponnesian War, 431 to 404 BCE
upsert.description: Athens and its empire fight Sparta and its allies for 27 years; plague kills perhaps a quarter of the Athenians (430 to 426), the expedition to Sicily is destroyed, and Sparta, with Persian money, wins; Thucydides writes its history.
provenance: sources to check: Thucydides; Kagan, The Peloponnesian War (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Greco-Persian Wars, 499 to 479 BCE
upsert.description: After the Ionian revolt, the Persian empire invades Greece twice; Athens wins at Marathon (490), Sparta's rearguard falls at Thermopylae, the Greek fleet wins at Salamis (480), and Plataea ends the invasion (479).
provenance: sources to check: Herodotus; Holland, Persian Fire (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Greece); Asia (Western Asia: Ionia)

upsert.boundary: The Punic Wars, 264 to 146 BCE
upsert.description: Rome and Carthage fight three wars for the western Mediterranean; Hannibal crosses the Alps and destroys a Roman army at Cannae (216), but Rome wins at Zama (202) and razes Carthage in 146.
provenance: sources to check: Goldsworthy, The Fall of Carthage (2000)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Italy, Sicily, Iberia); Africa (Northern Africa: Tunisia)

upsert.boundary: The Roman Empire, 27 BCE to 476 CE
upsert.description: Augustus founds a monarchy in republican dress; the empire rules some 60 to 70 million people, about a quarter of humanity, around the Mediterranean, with roads, cities, written law and two centuries of internal peace; in 212 all free men become citizens. It is divided into east and west, and the western empire falls to Germanic kings in the 400s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; population estimates range from about 45 to 75 million
sources to check: Scheidel (ed.), The Cambridge Economic History of the Greco-Roman World (2007)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern, Western and parts of Eastern and Northern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa); Asia (Western Asia)

upsert.boundary: The Roman Republic, 509 to 27 BCE
upsert.description: Rome expels its kings and governs through consuls, a senate and assemblies; it conquers Italy and then the Mediterranean, destroying Carthage and Corinth in 146 BCE; the wealth and armies of conquest breed civil wars that end with Julius Caesar's dictatorship and Augustus' victory.

upsert.boundary: The Western Roman Empire falls, 406 to 476
upsert.description: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine (406); Rome is sacked (410, 455) and its provinces and taxes are lost one by one, until Odoacer deposes the last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, in 476. Trade, cities, coinage and literacy shrink across the west for centuries.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; how far living standards fell is debated
sources to check: Ward-Perkins, The Fall of Rome and the End of Civilization (2005); Heather, The Fall of the Roman Empire (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Western and Southern Europe); Africa (Northern Africa)

upsert.boundary: Homo sapiens reaches Europe, about 47,000 to 43,000 years ago
upsert.description: Modern humans leave tools and bones at Bacho Kiro in Bulgaria and Ranis in Germany by about 45,000 years ago; early groups mix with Neanderthals (the Oase man had a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back) but most leave no descendants, and later arrivals become Europe's hunter-gatherers.
provenance: sources to check: Hublin et al. 2020, Nature 581; Mylopotamitaki et al. 2024, Nature 626; Fu et al. 2015, Nature 524

upsert.boundary: Herders from the steppe move into Europe, about 3000 to 2300 BCE
upsert.description: Yamnaya-descended herders with wagons, and perhaps plague, move west from the Pontic steppe; their descendants of the Corded Ware and Bell Beaker cultures replace most of the ancestry of central and northern Europe, in Britain some 90% within a few centuries, and probably carry the Indo-European languages.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the role of plague is debated
sources to check: Haak et al. 2015, Nature 522; Olalde et al. 2018, Nature 555; Rasmussen et al. 2015, Cell 163
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern, Central, Northern and Western Europe)

upsert.boundary: The eruption of Thera, about 1600 BCE
upsert.description: The volcano of Santorini erupts in one of the largest eruptions of the last ten thousand years, burying the Bronze Age town of Akrotiri in pumice and spreading ash over the eastern Mediterranean.
provenance: exploring: the date is disputed between about 1620 and 1530 BCE
sources to check: Manning, A Test of Time (2nd ed. 2014)

upsert.boundary: The gold of Varna, about 4600 to 4200 BCE
upsert.description: In a cemetery on the Black Sea coast, a few graves hold more gold than all others of their age combined: the oldest worked gold known, and among the first signs of a ranked elite.
provenance: sources to check: Higham et al. 2007, Antiquity 81

upsert.boundary: The Viking age, 793 to 1066
upsert.description: Scandinavian seafarers raid Lindisfarne (793) and then the coasts and rivers of Europe; they settle in Britain, Ireland and Normandy, found the Rus' state at Novgorod and Kyiv, trade as far as Baghdad, settle Iceland and Greenland, and reach North America at L'Anse aux Meadows about 1021.
provenance: sources to check: Price, Children of Ash and Elm (2020); Kuitems et al. 2022, Nature 601
upsert.region: Europe (Northern, Western and Eastern Europe); Americas (Northern America: Greenland, Newfoundland)

changes.value: Europe's own history to 1000, in its eras. Neanderthal Europe: the Last Interglacial and the signs of Neanderthal minds. The Upper Palaeolithic: Homo sapiens arrives, the Neanderthals disappear, the Campanian eruption, the first art, the Gravettians, the refuges of the glacial maximum and the Magdalenians. Mesolithic foragers and the first farmers: the foragers, Doggerland's drowning, the farmers from Anatolia, the mega-sites of Cucuteni–Trypillia, the gold of Varna and the megaliths. The Bronze Age: the steppe migrations, Minoan Crete, Thera and Mycenae. Classical antiquity: the alphabet, the Greek city-states, Greek philosophy, Athenian democracy, the Persian and Peloponnesian wars, the Roman Republic, the Punic wars, the Roman Empire and its third-century crisis, the rise of Christianity, Byzantium, the migration period and the fall of the west. The early Middle Ages: Justinian, the Franks, al-Andalus, the Vikings, the manor and the Christianization of the north. Two are world Events in humanity's eras: the alphabet and the rise of Christianity. The Roman Empire names the largest polity; the rise of Christianity and the conversion of the north name the Christian and local-religion shares. Existing Events that belong to Europe's history (the dispersal, farming, metallurgy, the horse and chariot, the Bronze Age collapse, the Axial age, Alexander, the Silk Roads, the Antonine and Justinianic plagues, the rise of Islam) are placed in its eras.

upsert.boundary: Radio and television, 1920 to 1990
upsert.description: From the first commercial radio broadcasts (1920) radio reaches most homes in rich countries by the 1930s and is used by Hitler and Roosevelt alike; television spreads from the 1950s, and by 1990 most of humanity is regularly reached by broadcast media.
provenance: sources to check: Briggs and Burke, A Social History of the Media (3rd ed. 2009)

upsert.boundary: Europe's agricultural revolution, about 1650 to 1850
upsert.description: First in the Low Countries and England, then across Europe, farmers grow clover and turnips in new rotations that feed more animals and fix nitrogen, enclose open fields and adopt the potato; yields roughly double, and the share of workers needed to grow food falls, from about three-quarters toward a third in England by 1800.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the timing of England's yield gains is debated
sources to check: Overton, Agricultural Revolution in England (1996); Allen, Enclosure and the Yeoman (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Berlin Wall falls, 9 November 1989
upsert.description: After months of protest and flight to the west, East Germany opens its border; crowds cross and break down the Wall, and within a year Germany is reunited.
provenance: sources to check: Sarotte, The Collapse (2014)

upsert.boundary: Europe's commercial revolution, about 1200 to 1500
upsert.description: Italian merchant cities develop banks, bills of exchange, partnerships, insurance and double-entry bookkeeping; the fairs of Champagne and the Hanseatic League of northern towns join the Mediterranean and the Baltic in one trading world.
provenance: sources to check: Lopez, The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages (1971); Spufford, Power and Profit (2002)

upsert.boundary: The Congress of Vienna, 1814 to 1815
upsert.description: The victorious powers redraw Europe's map and set up a concert of great powers that keeps a general peace for almost a century, broken by limited wars.
provenance: sources to check: Schroeder, The Transformation of European Politics 1763–1848 (1994)

upsert.boundary: Europe's births fall, about 1870 to 1939
upsert.description: After deaths fall, births follow: France's from about 1800, then across Europe from the 1870s, until by the 1930s many countries have about two children per woman and households shrink; it is the first demographic transition (DemographicTransition#6e31).
provenance: sources to check: Coale and Watkins (eds.), The Decline of Fertility in Europe (1986)

upsert.boundary: The Dutch Republic's golden age, 1581 to 1672
upsert.description: The northern Netherlands renounce Spanish rule (1581) and become the richest society in Europe: Amsterdam's exchange bank (1609) and stock exchange, the East India Company, the largest merchant fleet, religious toleration, and the painting of Rembrandt and Vermeer, until the French invasion of 1672.
provenance: sources to check: de Vries and van der Woude, The First Modern Economy (1997); Israel, The Dutch Republic (1995)

upsert.boundary: The war in the east, June 1941 to May 1945
upsert.description: Germany invades the Soviet Union in the largest war ever fought; after Moscow, Stalingrad and Kursk the Red Army drives to Berlin; some 27 million Soviet citizens die.
provenance: sources to check: Glantz and House, When Titans Clashed (2nd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The great European emigration, 1815 to 1914
upsert.description: Some 50 to 55 million Europeans, Irish, British, Germans, Scandinavians, Italians, Poles, Jews and others, leave for the Americas, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa, driven by land hunger, famine and persecution and drawn by wages, cheap land and steamships.
provenance: sources to check: Hatton and Williamson, The Age of Mass Migration (1998)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas; Oceania (Australia and New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The Enlightenment, 1687 to 1789
upsert.description: After Newton's Principia, writers from Locke and Voltaire to Montesquieu, Hume, Smith, Rousseau and Kant argue for reason, toleration, natural rights and the study of society, in salons, coffee houses, academies and the Encyclopédie.
provenance: sources to check: Robertson, The Enlightenment (2015); Israel, Radical Enlightenment (2001)

upsert.boundary: Europe's postwar expulsions, 1944 to 1950
upsert.description: As borders move west, some 12 to 14 million Germans flee or are expelled from Poland, Czechoslovakia and the east, and millions of Poles, Ukrainians and others are moved; perhaps half a million or more die.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; deaths are disputed
sources to check: Douglas, Orderly and Humane (2012)

upsert.boundary: Fascism in Europe, 1922 to 1945
upsert.description: Mussolini takes power in Italy (1922) and Hitler in Germany (1933), building one-party states of mass rallies, secret police and racial or national myth; Franco wins Spain's civil war (1939); fascist and allied regimes rule much of Europe until 1945.
provenance: sources to check: Paxton, The Anatomy of Fascism (2004); Evans, The Third Reich trilogy (2003 to 2008)

upsert.boundary: The fiscal-military state, about 1550 to 1815
upsert.description: Gunpowder fortresses, standing armies and navies multiply the cost of war; Europe's states that tax, borrow and administer most survive and absorb the rest (Warsift#b01b), so that the five hundred or so polities of 1500 shrink to about thirty by 1900, and Britain, France, Prussia, Austria and Russia emerge as great powers.
provenance: sources to check: Tilly, Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990); Brewer, The Sinews of Power (1989); Parker, The Military Revolution (1988)

upsert.boundary: The French Revolution, 1789 to 1799
upsert.description: Bankrupt after its wars, the monarchy calls the Estates-General; the Third Estate makes itself a National Assembly, Parisians storm the Bastille, the assembly abolishes feudal privileges and declares the Rights of Man; the king is executed (1793), the Terror follows, and war with Europe's monarchies brings Napoleon to power (1799).
provenance: sources to check: Doyle, The Oxford History of the French Revolution (2nd ed. 2002)

upsert.boundary: The East–West schism, 1054
upsert.description: Papal legates and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicate each other (July 1054), sealing a split between the Latin and Greek churches over papal authority, doctrine and rite that the Fourth Crusade's sack of Constantinople (1204) makes lasting.
provenance: sources to check: Chadwick, East and West: The Making of a Rift in the Church (2003)

upsert.boundary: The Holocaust, 1941 to 1945
upsert.description: Nazi Germany and its collaborators murder about six million Jews, two-thirds of Europe's Jews, by mass shootings in the east and in the gas chambers of Auschwitz, Treblinka and other death camps; Roma, disabled people and millions of Soviet prisoners and Polish civilians are also murdered.
provenance: sources to check: Hilberg, The Destruction of the European Jews (3rd ed. 2003); Friedländer, The Years of Extermination (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Soviet famine of 1932 to 1933
upsert.description: Forced collectivization and grain requisitions starve some five to seven million people, about four million in Ukraine, where the regime seals off the starving villages, and more than a million Kazakhs, nearly 40% of them.
provenance: sources to check: Davies and Wheatcroft, The Years of Hunger (2004); Applebaum, Red Famine (2017); Cameron, The Hungry Steppe (2018)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Ukraine, Russia); Asia (Central Asia: Kazakhstan)

upsert.boundary: Europe's long fall in homicide, about 1300 to 1950
upsert.description: Court and coroner records show homicide in European towns falling from perhaps 20 to 40 killings per 100,000 people a year in the 1300s to about one by the 1900s, first in England and the Low Countries, last in southern and eastern Europe, as states monopolize force, courts replace feuds and manners restrain men's violence.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; early rates rest on scattered local records
sources to check: Eisner 2003, Crime and Justice 30; Elias, The Civilizing Process (1939)

upsert.boundary: The Hundred Years' War, 1337 to 1453
upsert.description: The kings of England claim the throne of France and fight a long series of wars; English longbowmen win at Crécy and Agincourt, Joan of Arc revives the French cause, and France ends the English holdings by 1453 with cannon, a standing army and a permanent tax.
provenance: sources to check: Sumption, The Hundred Years War (1990 to 2015)
upsert.region: Europe (Western and Northern Europe: France, England)

upsert.boundary: Industrialization spreads across Europe, 1830 to 1914
upsert.description: Belgium, France, Germany, Switzerland and northern Italy follow Britain into coal, iron, textiles and machines, then Germany leads in steel, chemicals and electricity, and Russia industrializes from the 1890s; Europe's towns fill with factory workers.
provenance: sources to check: Pollard, Peaceful Conquest (1981)
upsert.region: Europe (Western, Northern, Southern and Eastern Europe)

upsert.boundary: European integration, from 1951
upsert.description: Six states pool coal and steel (1951) and found the European Economic Community (1957); it grows into a European Union of up to 28 members with a single market (1993), the euro (1999) and enlargement to the former communist east (2004); the euro crisis and Britain's exit (2020) test it.
provenance: sources to check: Dinan, Ever Closer Union (4th ed. 2010)
upsert.region: Europe (Western, Southern, Northern and Eastern Europe)

upsert.boundary: The Irish famine, 1845 to 1852
upsert.description: Potato blight destroys the crop of a people who live on it; about a million die of hunger and disease and over a million emigrate, while food is exported and relief is grudging; Ireland's population falls by a quarter and keeps falling for a century.
provenance: sources to check: Ó Gráda, Black '47 and Beyond (1999)

upsert.boundary: Europe divided by the Iron Curtain, 1946 to 1989
upsert.description: Soviet-backed communists take power across eastern Europe; Germany is split, NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) face each other, risings in Berlin (1953), Hungary (1956) and Prague (1968) are crushed, and the Berlin Wall (1961) closes the last gap.
provenance: sources to check: Judt, Postwar (2005); Applebaum, Iron Curtain (2012)

upsert.boundary: Jenner's smallpox vaccine, 1796 to 1802
upsert.description: Edward Jenner shows that cowpox protects against smallpox (May 1796); within a few years vaccination spreads across Europe and to the Americas and Asia, the start of the end of a disease that killed perhaps a tenth of Europeans.
provenance: sources to check: Riedel 2005, Baylor University Medical Center Proceedings 18

upsert.boundary: The labour movement and the first welfare laws, 1848 to 1914
upsert.description: Workers form unions, cooperatives and socialist parties, Marx and Engels publish the Communist Manifesto (1848), Bismarck's Germany introduces health, accident and old-age insurance (1883 to 1889), and campaigns for the eight-hour day cut the working week from over 70 hours toward 55.
provenance: sources to check: Eley, Forging Democracy (2002); Huberman 2004, Journal of Economic History 64

upsert.boundary: Europe's births fall below replacement, 1965 to 2025
upsert.description: After the baby boom, births per woman fall below two across Europe, to about 1.5 by the 2020s and below 1.3 in Italy, Spain and much of the east; households shrink, the population ages, and Europe's numbers would fall without immigration.
provenance: sources to check: Eurostat; UN World Population Prospects 2024

upsert.boundary: Magna Carta, June 1215
upsert.description: England's barons force King John to seal a charter limiting royal power, promising lawful judgment and no taxes without counsel; annulled within months, it is reissued and becomes a founding text of constitutional government.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, Magna Carta (3rd ed. 2015)

upsert.boundary: The European marriage pattern, about 1450 to 1850
upsert.description: West of a line from Trieste to St Petersburg, women marry late, at 23 to 27, many never marry, and couples set up their own households rather than joining their parents'; young people work for years as servants first. Late marriage limits births and leaves women time to earn.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its origin and economic effects are debated
sources to check: Hajnal 1965, in Population in History; De Moor and van Zanden 2010, Economic History Review 63

upsert.boundary: Mongol rule over Rus', 1237 to 1480
upsert.description: Batu's armies sack Ryazan, Vladimir and Kyiv (1237 to 1240); for more than two centuries the princes of Rus' pay tribute to the Golden Horde and receive their titles from it, while Moscow rises as its tax collector and ends the tribute after the stand on the Ugra (1480).
provenance: sources to check: Halperin, Russia and the Golden Horde (1985)

upsert.boundary: Napoleon's wars, 1799 to 1815
upsert.description: Napoleon seizes power, crowns himself emperor and conquers most of continental Europe, spreading his Civil Code and abolishing the Holy Roman Empire, until the retreat from Moscow (1812) and defeat at Leipzig and Waterloo (1815); some three to six million die.
provenance: sources to check: Bell, The First Total War (2007)

upsert.boundary: The Ottoman conquest of south-eastern Europe, 1354 to 1529
upsert.description: From Gallipoli (1354) the Ottomans take Thrace, defeat the Serbs at Kosovo (1389), take Constantinople (1453), the Balkans and, after Mohács (1526), most of Hungary, and besiege Vienna (1529); the Balkans remain Ottoman for four centuries.
provenance: sources to check: Finkel, Osman's Dream (2005)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern and Eastern Europe: the Balkans, Hungary)

upsert.boundary: The partitions of Poland, 1772 to 1795
upsert.description: Russia, Prussia and Austria divide the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in three steps, the last after a failed national rising, and Poland disappears from the map until 1918.
provenance: sources to check: Lukowski, The Partitions of Poland (1999)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Poland, Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine)

upsert.boundary: Peter the Great remakes Russia, 1682 to 1725
upsert.description: Peter studies shipyards in Holland and England, builds a navy and a conscript army, defeats Sweden in the Great Northern War, founds St Petersburg on the Baltic (1703), and forces Western dress, ranks and schools on the nobility, on the backs of an expanding serfdom.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, Russia in the Age of Peter the Great (1998)

upsert.boundary: Western Europe's postwar boom, 1948 to 1973
upsert.description: With Marshall aid, open trade, cheap oil and catching up with American technology, western Europe's economies grow by about 4 to 5% a year; most households gain cars, refrigerators and television, and a generation grows up without hunger or war, valuing self-expression over survival.
provenance: sources to check: Eichengreen, The European Economy since 1945 (2007); Inglehart, Cultural Evolution (2018)

upsert.boundary: Railways across Europe, 1825 to 1870
upsert.description: From the Stockton and Darlington (1825) and the Liverpool and Manchester (1830), railways spread across Europe; by 1870 there are over 100,000 kilometres of track, journeys that took days take hours, and markets, armies and newspapers move with them.
provenance: sources to check: Wolmar, Blood, Iron and Gold (2009)

upsert.boundary: The Renaissance, about 1350 to 1550
upsert.description: In the Italian cities, Petrarch and the humanists recover classical texts, Florence's Brunelleschi masters perspective and builds the cathedral dome, and Leonardo, Michelangelo and Raphael paint and sculpt for popes and bankers; through print and travel the movement spreads north.
provenance: sources to check: Burke, The European Renaissance (1998)
upsert.region: Europe (Southern Europe: Italy; Western and Northern Europe)

upsert.boundary: The revolutions of 1848
upsert.description: From Paris to Vienna, Berlin, Milan and Budapest, revolts demand constitutions, national unity and the end of serfdom; most are crushed within a year, but serfdom ends in Austria and the idea of the nation-state spreads.
provenance: sources to check: Sperber, The European Revolutions 1848–1851 (2nd ed. 2005)

upsert.boundary: Muscovy becomes Russia and crosses Siberia, 1552 to 1689
upsert.description: Ivan IV takes Kazan (1552) and Astrakhan, Cossacks and fur traders cross Siberia to the Pacific by 1639, and the Treaty of Nerchinsk (1689) fixes a border with Qing China: the largest country on Earth takes shape.
provenance: sources to check: Forsyth, A History of the Peoples of Siberia (1992)

upsert.boundary: The Russian revolutions and civil war, 1917 to 1922
upsert.description: Wartime collapse brings down the tsar (February 1917); Lenin's Bolsheviks seize power (October), take Russia out of the war and win a civil war of terror, famine and epidemics that kills perhaps eight to ten million, founding the Soviet Union (December 1922), a one-party state that persecutes religion.
provenance: sources to check: Smith, Russia in Revolution (2017)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern Europe: Russia, Ukraine, Belarus); Asia (Central Asia)

upsert.boundary: Europe secularizes, from about 1960
upsert.description: Church attendance collapses across western and northern Europe; by the 2020s only about one in ten attends weekly in most countries, and in several a majority say they have no religion.
provenance: sources to check: Bruce, Secularization (2011); Pew Research Center, Being Christian in Western Europe (2018)

upsert.boundary: Europe's share of humanity falls from 25% to 9%, 1910 to 2025
upsert.description: Two world wars, then births below replacement while Asia's, Latin America's and Africa's populations multiply: Europe's people grow from about 450 to some 745 million while humanity grows fivefold, and its share falls from a quarter to under a tenth.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares (1910 25.2%, 2025 9.1%)
sources to check: UN World Population Prospects 2024

upsert.boundary: Europe's share of humanity rises from 20% to 25%, 1750 to 1910
upsert.description: Better harvests, the potato, fewer famines and epidemics, and from the late 1800s cleaner water and medicine let Europe's population grow from about 160 million to over 450 million, faster than Asia's and Africa's, even as some 50 million Europeans emigrate overseas: its share peaks at about a quarter of humanity.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares (1750 20.5%, 1910 25.2%)
sources to check: Livi-Bacci, The Population of Europe (2000); UN historical estimates

upsert.boundary: The Soviet Union breaks up, 1991
upsert.description: After a failed hard-line coup (August 1991) the republics declare independence one by one, and the Soviet Union is dissolved on 26 December 1991 into fifteen states.
provenance: sources to check: Plokhy, The Last Empire (2014)
upsert.region: Europe (Eastern and Northern Europe); Asia (Central and Western Asia)

upsert.boundary: Stalin's Great Terror, 1936 to 1938
upsert.description: The NKVD arrests over 1.5 million people and shoots about 680,000, party leaders, officers, kulaks, national minorities and ordinary people alike, while the Gulag camps hold millions.
provenance: sources to check: Khlevniuk, The History of the Gulag (2004); Conquest, The Great Terror (1968)

upsert.boundary: The Thirty Years' War, 1618 to 1648
upsert.description: A Bohemian revolt grows into a war of most of Europe's powers fought mainly in Germany; armies living off the land, famine and plague kill perhaps a fifth of the German lands' people, more in some regions.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; losses vary greatly by region
sources to check: Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)
upsert.region: Europe (Western Europe: Germany; Eastern Europe: Bohemia)

upsert.boundary: Russia's war on Ukraine, from 2014
upsert.description: Russia annexes Crimea and backs a war in the Donbas (2014), then launches a full-scale invasion (February 2022); Ukraine holds Kyiv and retakes much ground, and the war becomes Europe's largest since 1945, with hundreds of thousands killed or wounded and millions of refugees.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; casualty figures are uncertain
sources to check: Plokhy, The Russo-Ukrainian War (2023)

upsert.boundary: Italy and Germany unified, 1859 to 1871
upsert.description: Piedmont, with French help and Garibaldi's volunteers, unites Italy (1861, Rome 1870); Bismarck's Prussia defeats Denmark, Austria and France and proclaims the German Empire at Versailles (January 1871).
provenance: sources to check: Breuilly, The Formation of the First German Nation-State (1996); Riall, Risorgimento (2009)

upsert.boundary: The first universities, about 1088 to 1300
upsert.description: Guilds of masters and students at Bologna, Paris and Oxford teach law, theology, medicine and the arts; scholars such as Thomas Aquinas reconcile Aristotle, newly translated from Arabic and Greek, with Christian teaching.
provenance: sources to check: Rashdall, The Universities of Europe in the Middle Ages; Grant, The Foundations of Modern Science in the Middle Ages (1996)

upsert.boundary: The Paris peace settlement, 1919 to 1920
upsert.description: The victors impose the Treaty of Versailles on Germany, with reparations and a war-guilt clause, break up Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman empire, create Poland, Czechoslovakia and Yugoslavia, and found the League of Nations.

upsert.boundary: Europe's wars of religion, 1562 to 1648
upsert.description: Catholics and Protestants fight across Europe: the French Wars of Religion (1562 to 1598), the Dutch Revolt against Spain (from 1568) and finally the Thirty Years' War, entangled with the rivalries of dynasties.
provenance: sources to check: Holt, The French Wars of Religion (2nd ed. 2005); Wilson, Europe's Tragedy (2009)

upsert.boundary: The welfare states, 1945 to 1980
upsert.description: Britain's National Health Service (1948), and pensions, unemployment insurance, family allowances and free education across western and northern Europe, give most people security from cradle to grave, paid for by taxes of 30 to 50% of national income.
provenance: sources to check: Esping-Andersen, The Three Worlds of Welfare Capitalism (1990); Lindert, Growing Public (2004)

upsert.boundary: The Peace of Westphalia, October 1648
upsert.description: The treaties of Münster and Osnabrück end the Thirty Years' War and the Eighty Years' War, recognize Dutch and Swiss independence and let German princes choose their territories' religion, in a settlement later read as the start of the system of sovereign states.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the 'Westphalian system' is partly a later myth
sources to check: Osiander 2001, International Organization 55

upsert.boundary: The European witch-hunts, about 1560 to 1680
upsert.description: Courts in the Holy Roman Empire, Scotland, Switzerland and elsewhere try perhaps 80,000 to 100,000 people for witchcraft and execute some 40,000 to 60,000, most of them women, at the height of the confessional wars.
provenance: sources to check: Levack, The Witch-Hunt in Early Modern Europe (4th ed. 2015); Leeson and Russ 2018, Economic Journal 128

upsert.boundary: The Yugoslav wars, 1991 to 2001
upsert.description: Yugoslavia breaks apart in wars in Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo and North Macedonia; some 130,000 to 140,000 die, millions are displaced by 'ethnic cleansing', and Bosnian Serb forces murder about 8,000 Muslim men and boys at Srebrenica (1995), a genocide.
provenance: sources to check: Glenny, The Fall of Yugoslavia (3rd ed. 1996); ICTY judgments

upsert.boundary: The global financial crisis, 2007 to 2009
upsert.description: Losses on American mortgage securities freeze credit; Lehman Brothers fails (September 2008), banks are rescued across the rich world, world output falls in 2009 for the first time since 1945, and Europe's debt crisis follows.

upsert.boundary: The Great Divergence, about 1800 to 1950
upsert.description: Industry lifts incomes in Western Europe and its settler offshoots far above those of Asia, Africa and Latin America, whose incomes stagnate or fall under colonial rule; income inequality between all the world's people, mostly between countries, rises to its highest.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its timing and causes are debated
sources to check: Pomeranz, The Great Divergence (2000); Bourguignon and Morrisson 2002, American Economic Review 92

upsert.boundary: The internet, from 1969
upsert.description: From ARPANET (1969) and TCP/IP (1983) through the World Wide Web, invented at CERN (1989 to 1991), and the smartphone (2007), the internet reaches about two-thirds of humanity by 2024, joining people, markets and knowledge in one network.
provenance: sources to check: Abbate, Inventing the Internet (1999); ITU, Facts and Figures 2024
upsert.region: Americas (Northern America); Europe; Asia; then everywhere

upsert.boundary: The Seven Years' War, 1756 to 1763
upsert.description: A war fought on four continents: Prussia survives Austria, France and Russia in Europe, while Britain takes Canada from France and wins in India and West Africa; the war's debts lead Britain to tax its American colonies and France toward bankruptcy.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Crucible of War (2000); Baugh, The Global Seven Years War (2011)
upsert.region: Europe; Americas (Northern America, the Caribbean); Asia (Southern Asia: India); Africa (Western Africa: Senegal)

upsert.boundary: Women win the vote, 1893 to 1971
upsert.description: New Zealand (1893), South Australia, Finland (1906) and Norway lead; after the First World War Britain, Germany, Russia and the United States follow; France and Italy after the Second, and Switzerland only in 1971.
provenance: sources to check: Paxton and Hughes, Women, Politics, and Power (3rd ed. 2016)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand); Europe; Americas

Europe's own history from 1000 to 2025, in its eras. The High and Late Middle Ages: the East–West schism, the universities, Magna Carta, the commercial revolution, Mongol rule in Rus', the Hundred Years' War, the Renaissance, the Ottoman conquest of the Balkans, the long fall of homicide and the European marriage pattern. The early modern era: the wars of religion and the Thirty Years' War, Westphalia, the fiscal-military state, the Dutch Republic, Russia's expansion, the witch-hunts, the agricultural revolution, Peter the Great, the Enlightenment, the Seven Years' War and the partitions of Poland. Revolution, industry and nations: Europe's share of humanity rises to 25%, the French Revolution and Napoleon, Jenner's vaccine, industrialization and the railways, emigration, the Irish famine, 1848, the labour movement, the unifications of Italy and Germany and the fall in births. The world wars: the Russian revolution, Versailles, fascism, the Soviet famine and terror, the Holocaust and the eastern front. Division and union: Europe's share falls to 9%, the expulsions, the Iron Curtain, the postwar boom and welfare states, integration, secularization, low fertility, the Berlin Wall, the Soviet collapse, the Yugoslav wars and the war in Ukraine. World Events in humanity's eras: the Seven Years' War, the Great Divergence, women's suffrage, broadcasting, the internet and the 2008 financial crisis. changes.value: Levels for Europe's Events on the scales for everyone, for Europe's own history, for the other regions they belong to and for their principal dimension. Europe's top level is held to ten Events: the arrival of farming, Greek philosophy, the Roman Empire, the rise of Christianity, the Black Death, the Reformation, the scientific revolution, the industrial revolution, the French Revolution and the Second World War. Europe's eras are frames: top_100 on Europe's scale, noted for everyone. Judged by consequence for later lives across the world, with hindsight held apart from what was known at the time (HindsightBlock#5d8d).

upsert.boundary: The heroic age of Antarctic exploration, 1897 to 1922
upsert.description: The Belgica's crew are the first to winter in the Antarctic (1898); Scott, Shackleton, Amundsen, Mawson and others sledge inland, reach the magnetic pole and the geographic pole, and Shackleton's Endurance is crushed in the ice (1915), its crew all saved.
provenance: sources to check: Fiennes, Race to the Pole (2004); Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)

upsert.boundary: Antarctica loses ice, from 1992
upsert.description: Satellites show Antarctica losing ice at an accelerating rate, about 150 billion tonnes a year by the 2010s, mostly from West Antarctic glaciers such as Thwaites and Pine Island; the Larsen B ice shelf breaks up in weeks (2002), and sea ice reaches record lows in 2023.
provenance: sources to check: IMBIE team 2018, Nature 558; Otosaka et al. 2023, Earth System Science Data 15

upsert.boundary: Antarctica's ice through the glacial cycles, before 11,700 years ago
upsert.description: The ice sheets, up to four kilometres thick, grow and shrink with the glacial cycles; the air trapped in their layers records 800,000 years of temperature and carbon dioxide, read in cores drilled from the 1960s on.
provenance: sources to check: EPICA community members 2004, Nature 429; Lüthi et al. 2008, Nature 453

upsert.boundary: The International Geophysical Year in Antarctica, 1957 to 1958
upsert.description: Twelve nations build some fifty research stations, among them the American station at the South Pole and the Soviet Vostok, and the Commonwealth Trans-Antarctic Expedition makes the first overland crossing; cooperation in science sets the pattern for the Treaty.
provenance: sources to check: Belanger, Deep Freeze (2006)

upsert.boundary: The Madrid Protocol bans mining in Antarctica, 1991 to 1998
upsert.description: The Treaty parties adopt an environmental protocol (October 1991, in force 1998) that designates Antarctica a natural reserve and forbids mining for at least fifty years.
provenance: sources to check: Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty (1991)

upsert.boundary: The ozone hole over Antarctica, from 1985
upsert.description: British Antarctic Survey scientists report that the ozone layer thins each spring over Antarctica (1985), caused by chlorofluorocarbons; the Montreal Protocol (1987) phases them out, and the hole begins slowly to heal, expected to close around 2066.
provenance: sources to check: Farman, Gardiner and Shanklin 1985, Nature 315; WMO Scientific Assessment of Ozone Depletion 2022

upsert.boundary: Sealing and whaling in the Southern Ocean, 1820 to 1986
upsert.description: Sealers nearly exterminate the fur seals of the sub-Antarctic islands by the 1830s; from South Georgia (1904) and then factory ships, whalers kill more than two million whales in the Southern Ocean in the twentieth century, until the International Whaling Commission's moratorium (1986).
provenance: sources to check: Rocha, Clapham and Ivashchenko 2014, Marine Fisheries Review 76
upsert.region: Antarctica (the Southern Ocean and sub-Antarctic islands)

upsert.boundary: Antarctica first sighted, January 1820
upsert.description: Within days of each other, Fabian von Bellingshausen's Russian expedition (27 January 1820) and Edward Bransfield's British one (30 January) sight the ice shelves and mountains of the continent; the first landing comes in 1821 or 1895.
provenance: sources to check: Headland, A Chronology of Antarctic Exploration (2009)

upsert.boundary: The race to the South Pole, December 1911 to January 1912
upsert.description: Roald Amundsen's Norwegian party, using dogs and skis, reaches the South Pole on 14 December 1911; Robert Falcon Scott's British party arrives on 17 January 1912 and dies on the return march.
provenance: sources to check: Huntford, Scott and Amundsen (1979)

upsert.boundary: Claims to Antarctica, 1908 to 1943
upsert.description: Britain (1908), New Zealand (1923), France (1924), Australia (1933), Norway (1939), Chile (1940) and Argentina (1943) claim wedges of the continent, three of them overlapping on the Peninsula; the United States and the Soviet Union reserve their own rights.
provenance: sources to check: Dodds, Geopolitics in Antarctica (1997)

upsert.boundary: The Antarctic Treaty, 1959 to 1961
upsert.description: Twelve nations sign in Washington (1 December 1959) a treaty, in force from June 1961, that freezes territorial claims, bans military activity, nuclear tests and waste, and reserves the continent for peace and science: the first arms-control treaty of the Cold War.
provenance: sources to check: Berkman et al. (eds.), Science Diplomacy (2011)

upsert.boundary: The Austronesian expansion, about 3000 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Rice- and millet-farming speakers of Austronesian languages sail from Taiwan into the Philippines and Indonesia, then east into the Pacific and west to Madagascar, in outrigger and double canoes; by 1300 their languages are spoken across more than half the globe's longitude, from Madagascar to Rapa Nui.
provenance: sources to check: Bellwood, First Islanders (2017); Gray, Drummond and Greenhill 2009, Science 323
upsert.region: Asia (Eastern Asia: Taiwan; South-eastern Asia); Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia, New Zealand); Africa (Eastern Africa: Madagascar)

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander rights, 1962 to 1993
upsert.description: Aboriginal people gain the federal vote (1962); the 1967 referendum counts them in the census and lets the Commonwealth make laws for them; land rights in the Northern Territory (1976) and the Mabo judgment (1992), which overturns 'terra nullius', lead to the Native Title Act (1993).
provenance: sources to check: Attwood, Rights for Aborigines (2003)

upsert.boundary: Māori Aotearoa before Cook, about 1280 to 1769
upsert.description: Polynesian settlers adapt to a cool, large land: they hunt moa and seals, then grow kumara and fern root, build fortified pā and form iwi and hapū that compete for land and mana, developing a Māori culture distinct from the tropical Pacific's.
provenance: sources to check: Anderson, Binney and Harris, Tangata Whenua (2014)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Pacific Islanders recruited for the Queensland cane fields, 1863 to 1906
upsert.description: Some 62,000 men and women from Vanuatu and the Solomon Islands are recruited, many by deception or force ('blackbirding'), to work on Queensland's sugar plantations; most are deported under the White Australia policy after 1906.
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia: Vanuatu, Solomon Islands; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: Rising seas threaten the atoll nations, from about 1990
upsert.description: With sea level rising and storm surges and salt intrusion worsening, Kiribati, Tuvalu and the Marshall Islands, whose land stands a few metres above the sea, plan for relocation; Tuvalu and Australia sign a treaty of climate mobility in 2023.
provenance: sources to check: IPCC AR6 WGII chapter 15 (Small Islands)

upsert.boundary: Cook's Pacific voyages, 1768 to 1779
upsert.description: James Cook observes the transit of Venus from Tahiti, charts New Zealand and the east coast of Australia (1770), crosses the Antarctic Circle and is killed in Hawaii (1779); his maps and reports open the Pacific to British settlement, trade and missions.
provenance: sources to check: Beaglehole, The Life of Captain James Cook (1974); Salmond, The Trial of the Cannibal Dog (2003)
upsert.region: Oceania (Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: Oceania's indigenous peoples decimated, 1788 to 1920
upsert.description: Smallpox, measles, influenza, venereal disease, violence and the loss of land cut Aboriginal Australians from perhaps 800,000 to under 100,000, Māori to about 42,000 (1896) and Hawaiians from some 300,000 to about 40,000 (1890), and many smaller island peoples by more; populations recover only in the 1900s.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; pre-contact numbers are uncertain
sources to check: Butlin, Our Original Aggression (1983); Pool, Te Iwi Maori (1991)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand; Polynesia; Melanesia)

upsert.boundary: Europeans enter the Pacific, 1521 to 1768
upsert.description: Magellan crosses the Pacific (1521); the Manila galleons cross it yearly from 1565; Spain conquers Guam and the Marianas in wars and epidemics that cut the Chamorro by nine-tenths; Tasman (1642) and Dutch captains chart Tasmania, New Zealand and the west of Australia.
provenance: sources to check: Spate, The Spanish Lake (1979)
upsert.region: Oceania (Micronesia: Guam; Australia and New Zealand); Europe

upsert.boundary: The Commonwealth of Australia, January 1901
upsert.description: Six colonies federate as the Commonwealth of Australia (1 January 1901); among the new parliament's first laws is the Immigration Restriction Act, the start of the White Australia policy.
provenance: sources to check: Irving, To Constitute a Nation (1997)

upsert.boundary: The First Fleet founds a convict colony at Sydney, January 1788
upsert.description: Eleven British ships land some 1,400 convicts, marines and officials at Sydney Cove (26 January 1788) on the land of the Gadigal people; Britain will send about 160,000 convicts to Australia by 1868.
provenance: sources to check: Hughes, The Fatal Shore (1987)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia); Europe (Northern Europe: Britain)

upsert.boundary: Australia's frontier wars, 1788 to 1934
upsert.description: As settlers and their flocks take land, Aboriginal peoples resist; hundreds of massacres, from the Black War in Tasmania (1824 to 1832) and Myall Creek (1838) to Coniston (1928), kill tens of thousands of Aboriginal people and a few thousand settlers.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; totals are disputed
sources to check: Reynolds, The Other Side of the Frontier (1981); Ryan et al., Colonial Frontier Massacres in Australia (2017 to 2022)

upsert.boundary: Gallipoli, April 1915 to January 1916
upsert.description: Australian and New Zealand troops land with the British and French on the Gallipoli peninsula to open the Dardanelles; after eight months and some 130,000 dead on both sides, the Allies withdraw. The landing becomes the founding legend of both nations (Anzac Day) and of Turkey's Atatürk.
upsert.region: Asia (Western Asia: Turkey); Oceania (Australia and New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The gold rushes of Australia and New Zealand, 1851 to 1900
upsert.description: Gold found in New South Wales and Victoria (1851), Otago (1861) and Western Australia (1890s) draws hundreds of thousands of migrants, including tens of thousands of Chinese; Victoria's population grows sevenfold in a decade and Melbourne becomes one of the richest cities in the world.
provenance: sources to check: Blainey, The Rush That Never Ended (5th ed. 2003)

upsert.boundary: Hawaii's chiefdoms become states, about 1600 to 1810
upsert.description: On the large Hawaiian islands, paramount chiefs claiming divine descent rule hierarchies of land divisions, irrigated taro and fishponds; Kamehameha, armed with European guns, unites the islands by 1810.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, How Chiefs Became Kings (2010)
upsert.region: Oceania (Polynesia: Hawaii, now a state of the United States)

upsert.boundary: The burials at Lake Mungo, about 42,000 to 40,000 years ago
upsert.description: On the shore of a lake now dry in western New South Wales, a young woman is cremated and a man is buried sprinkled with red ochre: among the oldest known burials of Homo sapiens anywhere, returned to their people in 2017 and 1992.
provenance: sources to check: Bowler et al. 2003, Nature 421

upsert.boundary: Lapita voyagers settle Remote Oceania, about 1300 to 800 BCE
upsert.description: Potters who decorate their wares with dentate stamps spread from the Bismarck Archipelago to Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa within a few centuries, crossing gaps of hundreds of kilometres to islands no one had reached before; they are the ancestors of the Polynesians.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017)

upsert.boundary: Macassan trepangers in northern Australia, about 1720 to 1906
upsert.description: Fleets of praus from Makassar in Sulawesi sail each monsoon to Arnhem Land and the Kimberley to gather and cure sea cucumbers for the Chinese market, trading cloth, metal and tobacco with Yolngu and other peoples, until Australia bans them in 1906.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; the start may be earlier
sources to check: Macknight, The Voyage to Marege' (1976)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: northern Australia); Asia (South-eastern Asia: Sulawesi)

upsert.boundary: Sahul's giant animals die out, about 46,000 to 40,000 years ago
upsert.description: Diprotodon, the rhino-sized marsupial, giant kangaroos, the flightless bird Genyornis and giant lizards disappear within some thousands of years of people's arrival; hunting, burning and a drying climate are all blamed.
provenance: exploring: timing and causes are debated
sources to check: Roberts et al. 2001, Science 292; Saltré et al. 2016, Nature Communications 7
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia; Melanesia: New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: The moa hunted to extinction, about 1300 to 1450
upsert.description: Within about 150 years of people's arrival, all nine species of moa, giant flightless birds up to 3.6 metres tall, and the Haast's eagle that preyed on them are gone: one of the fastest human-caused extinctions known.
provenance: sources to check: Perry et al. 2014, Quaternary Science Reviews 105; Holdaway et al. 2014, Nature Communications 5
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: Nan Madol and the Saudeleur dynasty, about 1180 to 1628
upsert.description: On a reef off Pohnpei, rulers who unite the island build nearly a hundred artificial islets of stacked basalt columns, a ceremonial and royal centre, until the Saudeleurs are overthrown.
provenance: sources to check: McCoy et al. 2016, Quaternary Research 86

upsert.boundary: Farming begins in the New Guinea highlands, about 8000 to 4500 BCE
upsert.description: At Kuk Swamp highland people dig drains and mound gardens and cultivate taro, bananas and yams, one of the world's independent inventions of farming; sugarcane and some bananas spread from here across the tropics.
provenance: sources to check: Denham et al. 2003, Science 301

upsert.boundary: Nuclear tests in the Pacific and Australia, 1946 to 1996
upsert.description: The United States explodes 67 weapons at Bikini and Enewetak (1946 to 1958), displacing islanders and contaminating Rongelap; Britain tests at Maralinga and Christmas Island, and France at Moruroa and Fangataufa until 1996.
provenance: sources to check: Firth, Nuclear Playground (1987)
upsert.region: Oceania (Micronesia: Marshall Islands, Kiribati; Polynesia: French Polynesia; Australia and New Zealand: Australia)

upsert.boundary: The New Zealand Wars, 1845 to 1872
upsert.description: Disputes over land sales become wars between the colonial government and Māori iwi in the North Island; after the wars the government confiscates millions of acres, and settlers soon outnumber Māori.
provenance: sources to check: Belich, The New Zealand Wars (1986)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

upsert.boundary: The Pacific divided among empires, 1842 to 1900
upsert.description: France takes Tahiti (1842) and New Caledonia (1853), Britain Fiji (1874) and part of New Guinea, Germany north-east New Guinea, the Marshalls and Samoa, and the United States annexes Hawaii (1898) after American planters overthrow its queen (1893); by 1900 hardly an island is independent.
provenance: sources to check: Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia); Europe; Americas (Northern America: the United States)

upsert.boundary: The Pacific island nations become independent, 1962 to 1980
upsert.description: Samoa (1962) is first, then Nauru (1968), Tonga's full sovereignty and Fiji (1970), Papua New Guinea (1975), Solomon Islands and Tuvalu (1978), Kiribati (1979) and Vanuatu (1980); others remain territories or freely associated states.
provenance: sources to check: Fischer, A History of the Pacific Islands (2nd ed. 2013)

upsert.boundary: The war in the Pacific islands, December 1941 to 1945
upsert.description: Japan takes New Guinea's north coast, the Solomons and the Gilberts and bombs Darwin (1942); Kokoda, Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan and Peleliu are fought on islanders' land, with tens of thousands of Pacific Islanders killed, conscripted or displaced.
provenance: sources to check: White and Lindstrom (eds.), The Pacific Theater (1989)
upsert.region: Oceania (Melanesia, Micronesia; Australia and New Zealand); Asia (Eastern Asia: Japan)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians settle the eastern Pacific, about 900 to 1300
upsert.description: After a pause of nearly two thousand years in Samoa and Tonga, voyagers navigating by stars, swells and birds settle the Society Islands and the Marquesas, then within a few centuries Hawaii, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa New Zealand (about 1280), the last large land on Earth to be peopled.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; dates follow the 'short chronology'
sources to check: Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108

upsert.boundary: Postwar migration remakes Australia and New Zealand, from 1945
upsert.description: Under 'populate or perish', Australia takes millions of migrants from Britain, then southern and eastern Europe; the White Australia policy ends (1973) and migrants from Asia follow, until nearly a third of Australians are born overseas; Oceania grows from about 13 to 46 million people.
provenance: sources to check: Jupp, From White Australia to Woomera (2nd ed. 2007); Australian Bureau of Statistics

upsert.boundary: Rapa Nui and its moai, about 1200 to 1722
upsert.description: On the most isolated inhabited island on Earth, clans carve and raise nearly a thousand stone statues of their ancestors while the island's palm forest disappears; whether the society collapsed in an ecological catastrophe or adapted and endured until European disease and slave raids is disputed.
provenance: exploring: collapse versus resilience is debated
sources to check: Diamond, Collapse (2005); Hunt and Lipo, The Statues That Walked (2011); DiNapoli et al. 2020, Nature Communications 11
upsert.region: Oceania (Polynesia: Rapa Nui, now part of Chile)

upsert.boundary: Aboriginal rock art and the Dreaming, from about 28,000 years ago
upsert.description: From the charcoal drawings of Nawarla Gabarnmang (about 28,000 years old) to the Gwion figures of the Kimberley and the X-ray paintings of Arnhem Land, Aboriginal peoples record on rock the ancestral beings, laws and country of the Dreaming, the oldest continuous artistic tradition on Earth.
provenance: sources to check: David et al. 2013, Journal of Archaeological Science 40; Taçon and Chippindale (eds.), The Archaeology of Rock-Art (1998)

upsert.boundary: People reach Sahul, about 50,000 years ago
upsert.description: Crossing at least 70 kilometres of open sea through the islands of Wallacea, the first people reach Sahul, the continent that joined Australia, New Guinea and Tasmania at low sea level; the earliest secure sites date to about 50,000 years ago, and Madjedbebe in Arnhem Land may be 65,000 years old. Their descendants are the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and Papuan peoples.
provenance: exploring: the earliest date is contested, from about 65,000 to 47,000 years ago
sources to check: Clarkson et al. 2017, Nature 547; O'Connell et al. 2018, PNAS 115
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: Australia; Melanesia: New Guinea)

upsert.boundary: Rising seas split Sahul, about 10,000 to 6000 BCE
upsert.description: As the ice melts, Bass Strait floods and cuts Tasmania off, and then the Torres Strait separates New Guinea from Australia; the Tasmanians live apart from all other people for some ten thousand years.
provenance: sources to check: Lambeck and Chappell 2001, Science 292

upsert.boundary: Settlers multiply Oceania's people, 1788 to 1950
upsert.description: Convicts, assisted migrants, gold-seekers and their children grow Australia's and New Zealand's settler populations from nothing to about 10 million by 1950, while the indigenous peoples shrink: Oceania's share of humanity rises from about 0.2% to 0.5%.
provenance: inferred: from the model's own regional shares
sources to check: Australian Bureau of Statistics historical population; UN historical estimates

upsert.boundary: The stolen generations, about 1910 to 1970
upsert.description: Under government policies of 'protection' and assimilation, perhaps one in ten to one in three Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children are taken from their families and raised in institutions or by white families; a national apology follows in 2008.
provenance: sources to check: Bringing Them Home report (1997)

upsert.boundary: Polynesians and South Americans meet, about 1150 to 1230
upsert.description: Native South American ancestry in the genomes of eastern Polynesians, dated to about 1200, and the sweet potato grown across Polynesia before Europeans came, show that Polynesian voyagers reached South America or South Americans reached Polynesia.
provenance: sources to check: Ioannidis et al. 2020, Nature 583

upsert.boundary: The maritime chiefdom of Tonga, about 1200 to 1500
upsert.description: The Tu'i Tonga, sacred paramount chiefs, build great stone tombs at Lapaha and extend their influence by voyaging and marriage over Samoa, 'Uvea, Fiji and beyond, the largest political network in Polynesia.
provenance: inferred: as recalled; its extent is debated
sources to check: Clark, Burley and Murray 2008, Antiquity 82

upsert.boundary: The Treaty of Waitangi, February 1840
upsert.description: British officials and some 500 Māori chiefs sign a treaty whose English text cedes sovereignty and whose Māori text, te Tiriti, promises chiefs continued authority over their lands; the gap between them shapes New Zealand's politics ever after.
provenance: sources to check: Orange, The Treaty of Waitangi (2nd ed. 2011)
upsert.region: Oceania (Australia and New Zealand: New Zealand)

changes.value: Oceania's and Antarctica's own histories, in their eras. Ancient Sahul: the first people, the extinction of the megafauna, Lake Mungo, rock art and the Dreaming, the rising seas that split Sahul, and farming in New Guinea. Lapita and the settling of Remote Oceania: the Austronesian expansion (a world Event, from Taiwan to Madagascar and Aotearoa), Lapita, the settlement of Polynesia and its meeting with South America. The island kingdoms: Nan Madol, Tonga, Rapa Nui, Aotearoa and the moa, Hawaii, the first Europeans and the Macassan trepangers. Contact and colonization: Cook, the First Fleet, the frontier wars, the collapse of indigenous populations, Waitangi and the New Zealand wars, the gold rushes, blackbirding, the partition of the Pacific and settler growth. Federation and the island nations: federation, Gallipoli, the stolen generations, the Pacific war, the nuclear tests, independence, postwar migration, Aboriginal rights and rising seas. Antarctica: the ice through the glacial cycles, first sighting, sealing and whaling, the heroic age and the South Pole, territorial claims, the International Geophysical Year, the Treaty, the ozone hole, the Madrid Protocol and the loss of ice. The Events that turn Oceania's share of humanity name it: the arrival of people, settler growth and postwar migration.

upsert.boundary: The Last Interglacial and its aftermath, about 132,000 to 62,000 years ago
upsert.description: The interglacial proper, warmer than today, ends about 116,000 years ago; the era runs on through the milder stretches of the early last glacial that followed. A green Sahara and Arabia open corridors: Homo sapiens reaches the Levant (Skhul and Qafzeh) and perhaps Arabia and beyond, but those groups leave few descendants. In southern Africa coastal groups make engraved ochre and shell beads (Blombos, about 75,000 years ago) and the Still Bay and Howiesons Poort toolkits. As the glacial returns after about 71,000 years ago, populations shrink and fragment.
provenance: sources to check: Henshilwood et al. 2002, Science 295 (Blombos engravings); Groucutt et al. 2015, Evolutionary Anthropology 24 (routes out of Africa)

inferred: corrected 2026-10-13 after a blind reading of the events pass: the interglacial proper (marine isotope stage 5e) ends about 116,000 years ago; the era is named for it and its aftermath, as its boundary says

upsert.boundary: The High and Late Middle Ages, 1000 to 1500
upsert.description: Europe's people double; towns, fairs, guilds and universities grow; the Great Schism (1054); the Norman conquest of England (1066); the Crusades (1096 to 1291); Magna Carta (1215); the Mongols take Rus (1237 to 1240); the Great Famine (1315) and the Black Death (in Europe 1347 to 1351; the whole pandemic 1346 to 1353); the Hundred Years' War; the Ottomans take Constantinople (1453); the Renaissance begins in Italy; printing; the Reconquista ends (1492).
provenance: sources to check: Bartlett, The Making of Europe (1993); Jordan, Europe in the High Middle Ages (2001)
inferred: corrected 2026-10-13 after a blind reading of the events pass: the Black Death's dates for Europe given beside the pandemic's own (ev.black-death)

upsert.boundary: Lapita and the settling of Remote Oceania, about 1500 BCE to 1300 CE
upsert.description: Austronesian-speaking voyagers with pottery, pigs, chickens and outrigger canoes, the Lapita culture, reach the Bismarcks about 1350 BCE, then Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE; Micronesia is settled from the Philippines and from Melanesia; the dingo arrives in Australia. After a long pause East Polynesia is settled in a burst from about 1000 CE: the Society Islands, Hawai'i, Rapa Nui and Aotearoa last, about 1280. The sweet potato, a South American plant, is growing in East Polynesia before Europeans arrive, and Native American ancestry dated to about 1200 is found in East Polynesians: contact with South America is likely, but whether Polynesians sailed there and back or South Americans reached Polynesia is debated.
provenance: sources to check: Kirch, On the Road of the Winds (2nd ed. 2017); Wilmshurst et al. 2011, PNAS 108 (East Polynesian chronology); Ioannidis et al. 2020, Nature 583 (contact with the Americas)

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"observation","text":"Between -151000 and -127000 sea level rises 110 m, temperature 6 °C, CO2 from 190 to 275 ppm and forest from 36 to 47% of land. This is Termination II, into the Last Interglacial, warmer than pre-industrial and with seas several metres higher. Humanity's numbers are guessed to rise with it (0.35 to 0.5 million), because a green Sahara and Arabia opened ranges that the glacial had closed. The early sapiens fossils outside Africa, such as Misliya and Skhul, fall in or near such windows; the model has no regional processes yet to show it."}
upsertNodes.title: The sharpest change at the finest level: the end of the penultimate glacial

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"revision","text":"The first pass gave the eight religion shares as anchors at -300000 and -1000 and interpolated them linearly onto its dates. Between those anchors that put 1.3% of people in the Hindu tradition and 0.9% in Chinese traditions 100,000 years ago, and 3% Hindu in 5000 BCE: no one claimed this, the arithmetic did. Every share before 1000 BCE is now local and folk traditions at 100%, at the old dates and the new. The jump to the anchor at -1000 (95, 3, 0, 2) now stands for the Vedic and Zhou traditions forming, which is a claim. The general lesson for whoever fills next: interpolating between anchors far apart makes claims about the dates between, so guess those dates instead."}

upsertNodes.text: {"schema":"meaning-model-understanding-note/v1","kind":"revision","text":"Time -10000 is about 12,000 years before present, inside the Younger Dryas. Global reconstructions of the deglaciation, Shakun and colleagues' as recalled, reach Holocene levels only about 10,000 years ago. The first pass's -1.5 °C put the world most of the way there two thousand years early. The new -12000 value (-3.5 °C, the Bølling–Allerød) and -7900 (-0.8 °C) are guessed around the revised one."}
